title: Washington v. Ohlson
facts: Petitioner James Ohlson was convicted of two counts of second degree assault in the Superior Court for Kitsap County after a trial in which one victim testified and the out of court statement of the other victim was admitted into evidence in lieu of their testimony. Ohlson appealed his conviction, asserting that the admission of the out of court statement infringed his right under the 6th Amendment to the United States Constitution to be confronted with the witnesses against him. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Ohlson’s conviction, holding that the out of court statement, which was made to a police officer arriving at the scene shortly after the assault, was an excited utterance and therefore non-testimonial in nature. Ohlson appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court infringe Ohlson’s right to be confronted with the witnesses against him by admitting the victim’s out of court statement into evidence?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although excited utterances are not necessarily non-testimonial in nature, the victim’s out of court statement, which was made to enable police assistance to meet an ongoing emergency, was non-testimonial and properly admitted.

title: In re personal restraint of Shale
facts: Petitioner Cole Shale pled guilty to three counts of first degree possession of stolen property and three counts of unlawful possession of payment instruments in the Superior Court for Spokane County. Shale subsequently moved to vacate his convictions and sentence on grounds that his offenses constitute a single unit of prosecution and that his offender score was improperly calculated. The superior court transferred the case to the Washington Court of Appeals for consideration as a personal restraint petition. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Shale’s convictions and sentence. Shale appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Shale’s multiple convictions subject him to double jeopardy in violation of the 5th Amendment to the United States Constitution? Should Shale’s convictions have been treated as the “same criminal conduct” for purposes of calculating his offender score?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Shale’s plea agreement was an indivisible package agreement and that Shale cannot raise the double jeopardy issue without moving to withdraw all of his pleas. The Court also held that Shale cannot challenge the calculation of his offender score insofar as Shale failed to raise the factual issue of whether his convictions constitute the “same criminal conduct” prior to his sentencing.

title: Udall v. T.D. Escrow Services, Inc.
facts: Lender U.S. Bancorp directed respondent T.D. Escrow Services, Inc. to commence foreclosure proceedings on a property after the borrower defaulted. T.D. Escrow Services proceeded to employ A.B.C. Legal Services to conduct the foreclosure sale. At the subsequent auction, petitioner William Udall was the high bidder and was given a receipt but not the deed of trust for the property. When T.D. Escrow Services discovered that A.B.C. Legal Services had erroneously sold the property to Udall at a price $100,000 lower than it had authorized, it refused to deliver the deed of trust to Udall. Udall responded by filing suit to quiet title. The trial court granted summary judgment for Udall. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the sale of the property had not been completed under the terms of Washington’s deed of trust act (Washington Revised Code §61.24) and that T.D. Escrow Services was therefore not required to deliver the deed of trust to Udall. Udall appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §61.24 require that a trustee deliver the deed of trust to the purchaser of a property following a foreclosure sale?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and ordered that title be quieted in Udall, concluding that under §61.24 a property is considered sold once the trustee accepts a bid unless there is a procedural irregularity that voids the sale. Thus, as deficiency in price alone is insufficient basis for setting aside a sale on grounds of procedural irregularity, the Court held that §61.24 requires that T.D. Escrow Services deliver the deed of trust to Udall.

title: Ehsani v. McCullough Family Partnership
facts: After a judgment in which respondent Sayed Zia Ehsani had to pay money into David C. Cullen’s client trust account, Cullen distributed the funds under his clients’ direction (petitioner McCullough Family Partnership) to the clients’ creditors, including himself for legal services rendered. Ehsani successfully appealed and the trial court’s judgment was reversed. On remand Ehsani filed a motion in King County Superior Court for restitution pursuant to Wash. RAP 12.8, asking the court to restore the funds Cullen previously distributed from his client trust account. The trial court denied the motion for restitution, and Ehsani appealed. The Division One Court of Appeals held that the trial court erred in denying Ehsani’s Wash. RAP 12.8 motion, and that Cullen is liable to Ehsani in restitution for the full amount since the funds were distributed from his client trust account. Cullen subsequently petitioned for review to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the case present the “appropriate circumstances” according to Wash. RAP 12.8 for post-appeal restitution? Did the trial court abuse its discretion in denying Eshani’s motion for restitution? Is Cullen liable to restore the funds that were dispersed from his client trust account?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson's opinion for the Court concluded that the Court of Appeals erred in its reversal of the trial court’s denial of Ehsani’s motion for restitution. According to the Wash. RAP 12.8, the case does not present the “appropriate circumstances” necessary for an award of restitution in which Cullen would be liable to restore the funds dispersed from his client trust account. Because of the vague language in Wash. RAP 12.8, the trial court had full discretionary authority to determine if the motion for restitution should be denied, and thus did not abuse it discretion. Cullen was a bone fide creditor of his clients and did not receive payments pursuant to a statutory scheme making him a real party of interest. Instead, Cullen was paid by the initial judgment creditors, his clients, for legal services rendered. The fact that these funds were held and distributed from Cullen’s client trust account does not alter this analysis, and thus he is not liable in restitution to Ehsani.

title: Stewart-Graves v. Vaughn
facts: Petitioner Nichole Stewart-Graves’ son Liam was born without a heartbeat or spontaneous respiration but was eventually resuscitated by respondent Katherine Vaughn, the attending physician. However, due to the fact that he was not breathing for over twenty minutes before Vaughn succeeded in resuscitating him, Liam was left with severe brain damage and other disabilities. Stewart-Graves subsequently filed a medical malpractice action against Vaughn in the Superior Court for Clark County, asserting that Vaughn failed to obtain informed consent to continue resuscitation after ten minutes, at which point it was no longer reasonably possible for Liam to survive without severe brain damage, and that Vaughn breached the applicable standard of care by not discontinuing resuscitation at that point. The trial court granted summary judgment for Vaughn. Stewart-Graves appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Vaughn required to obtain informed consent to continue resuscitation of Liam Stewart-Graves after it was no longer reasonably possible for Liam to survive without severe brain damage? Did the applicable standard of care require that Vaughn discontinue resuscitation at that point?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court, concluding that Vaughn was not required to obtain informed consent to continue resuscitating Liam Stewart-Graves as there was no opportunity for a deliberate and informed decision to refuse consent insofar as any delay would have resulted in Liam’s certain and immediate death. The Court also held that the applicable standard of care does not require a healthcare provider to withhold treatment of a newborn infant based upon the likelihood that the infant will be severely disabled if it survives.

title: Washington v. Day
facts: Petitioner Charlie Day was convicted of the manufacture of methamphetamine in the Superior Court for Benton County after a search of his automobile occasioned by it being illegally parked revealed evidence of methamphetamine manufacturing. Day appealed his conviction, asserting that the warrantless search of his automobile lacked probable cause. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Day’s conviction, holding that the search was based upon a reasonable suspicion that Day was engaged in criminal activity given that the police officer who found Day parked illegally noticed drug paraphernalia and an empty handgun case in Day’s automobile during their questioning of Day. Day appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May a police officer detain a suspect for questioning when their initial contact with the suspect arises from a parking infraction?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that a police officer may not detain a suspect for questioning when they merely suspect a parking infraction. Thus, the Court ordered evidence derived from the search of Day’s automobile suppressed and remanded the case.

title: Washington v. Benn
facts: Respondent Gary Benn was convicted of two counts of aggravated murder in the Superior Court for Pierce County. With regard to the presence of aggravating factors, the jury found that the murders were part of a common scheme or plan but did not return a verdict as to whether the murders were committed as a single act. Benn’s convictions were subsequently vacated on appeal and the state of Washington retried Benn. Benn was once again found guilty and the jury also found that the murders were committed as a single act. Consequently, Benn was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Benn appealed his sentence, asserting that he was subjected to double jeopardy when the state realleged the “single act” aggravating factor as the jury’s failure to return a verdict as to whether this aggravating factor was present in his first trial constituted an implied acquittal. The Washington Court of Appeals vacated Benn’s sentence and remanded the case for resentencing. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Benn subjected to double jeopardy when the state retried the issue of whether the “single act” aggravating factor was present?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and reinstated Benn’s sentence, concluding that double jeopardy principles do not apply to individual aggravating factors and that the jury’s failure to return a verdict as to whether the “single act” aggravating factor was present therefore did not constitute an acquittal for double jeopardy purposes.

title: Washington v. Vander Houwen
facts: Petitioner Jerrie Vander Houwen was convicted of two counts of killing game out of season in the District Court for Yakima County after killing a number of elk that were damaging his cherry and apple orchards. Vander Houwen subsequently appealed his convictions, asserting that the trial court had erred in failing to instruct the jury that killing game out of season is not a crime if reasonably necessary for the defense of one’s property and in failing to associate evidence collected from specific dead elk found on Vander Houwen’s property with specific counts of killing game out of season. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Vander Houwen’s convictions. Vander Houwen appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court err in its instruction to the jury regarding the defense of necessity? Did the trial court err in failing to associate evidence collected from specific dead elk found on Vander Houwen’s property with specific counts of killing game out of season?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and vacated Vander Houwen’s convictions, concluding that the trial court should have instructed the jury that killing game out of season is not a crime if reasonably necessary for the defense of one’s property and that the trial court’s instruction to the jury regarding the defense of necessity improperly shifted the burden of proof to Vander Houwen by requiring him to prove that his actions were necessary rather than requiring the state to prove that they were not. The Court also held that the trial court erred in failing to associate evidence collected from specific dead elk found on Vander Houwen’s property with specific counts of killing game out of season as the fact that Vander Houwen was acquitted of eight of the ten charges of killing game out of season against him made it impossible to ensure that all of the jurors voted to convict him on the basis of the same two dead elk.

title: Potter v. Washington State Patrol
facts: After he was found driving with a suspended driver’s license, petitioner Mark Potter’s automobile was impounded by the respondent Washington State Patrol pursuant to the mandatory impoundment policy established by Washington Administrative Code §204-96-010. Following the Supreme Court of Washington’s decision in All Around Underground, Inc. v. Washington State Patrol, in which the Court held that §204-96-010 is an unlawful exercise of the statutory authority granted to the Washington State Patrol in Washington Revised Code §46.55.113, Potter filed a class action lawsuit against the Washington State Patrol on behalf of himself and all of the owners of automobiles impounded pursuant to §204-96-010. The trial court granted summary judgment for the Washington State Patrol, ruling that an action for conversion cannot be brought against the Washington State Patrol insofar as its actions were authorized by law and reasonable. Potter appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May the Washington State Patrol be held liable for conversion for impoundments carried out under the authority of §204-96-010 prior to the Supreme Court of Washington’s decision in All Around Underground, Inc. v. Washington State Patrol?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the trial court and remanded the case, concluding that while the fact that the Washington State Patrol’s actions were authorized by law and reasonable immunizes its officers from liability, it does not immunize the Washington State Patrol as an organization from liability for promulgating a regulation that exceeded its statutory authority.

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Carpenter
facts: Petitioner Timothy Carpenter was charged with two counts of misconduct by the Washington State Bar Association’s Disciplinary Board arising out of his representation of two codefendents in a lawsuit to collect on a property transaction. The Disciplinary Board recommended Carpenter be suspended from practicing law for two months for knowing violations of Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §1.7 and §1.9 for failing to withdraw when it became clear the codefendents had a conflict of interest, and §1.15(a) for representing one codefentent against the other in a later indemnification action without obtaining a consent or waiver allowing Carpenter’s involvement in the litigation. Carpenter appealed, claiming he acted out of negligence and the Disciplinary Board’s recommended sanction was inappropriate.
questions: Did Carpenter knowingly violate Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §1.7 and §1.9 under the first charge, and §1.15(a) under the second charge? Is the Disciplinary Board’s recommended sanction appropriate after balancing the mitigating and aggravating factors?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court upheld the Disciplinary Board’s recommended sanction, holding that Carpenter should have obtained a fully informed written consent from his former client allowing his involvement. The burden is on the attorney to do so when there is the possibility of conflicting interests, not on the client. Similarly, Carpenter had to undoubtedly know there was a conflict of interest between the codefendents, and should have withdrawn from representation. The Disciplinary Board correctly found that the aggravating factors of Carpenter’s legal experience, the multiple offenses involved, and the potential harm to the client, when weighed against the mitigating factors, provides substantial evidence to prove Carpenter committed knowing violations of Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §1.7, §1.9, and §1.15(a). The Court affirmed the Disciplinary Board’s recommendation of a two month suspension.

title: Woods v. Kittitas County
facts: Petitioner Cecile Woods filed suit against respondent Kittitas County in the Superior Court for Kittitas County pursuant to the Land Use Petition Act (Washington Revised Code §36.70C). Woods sought the reversal of the Kittitas County Commission’s decision to rezone a parcel of land from forest and range to rural. The superior court granted the petition and reversed the rezone, ruling that it was inconsistent with the Growth Management Act (Washington Revised Code §36.70A). Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the superior court lacked subject matter jurisdiction to decide whether the rezone is consistent with the Growth Management Act. Woods appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the superior court have jurisdiction to decide whether the rezone is consistent with the Growth Management Act?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that a Land Use Petition Act challenge to a site-specific land use decision can only be for violations of a comprehensive plan or for violations of development regulations and that the superior court therefore lacked jurisdiction to decide whether the rezone is consistent with the Growth Management Act. Turning to the remaining issues raised by Woods, the Court held that the rezone was supported by substantial evidence and was not based upon an erroneous interpretation of the law or a clearly erroneous application of the law to the facts.

title: Potter vs. Washington State Patrol
facts: After petitioner Mark Potter was cited for driving with a suspended driver’s license, his automobile was impounded and eventually auctioned by the respondent Washington State Patrol pursuant to the procedures outlined in Washington Administrative Code §204-96-010. Asserting that his automobile had been unlawfully converted, Potter filed a class action suit against the Washington State Patrol on behalf of himself and all of the owners of automobiles impounded pursuant to §204-96-010. The trial court granted the Washington State Patrol’s motion for summary judgment, ruling that the Washington State Patrol’s exercise of authority in impounding and auctioning Potter’s automobile was privileged and that it therefore could not be held liable for conversion. Upon appeal, the Supreme Court of Washington reversed, holding that the Washington State Patrol’s exercise of its authority was not privileged. The Washington State Patrol moved for reconsideration to review whether Washington Revised Code §46.55 bars Potter’s action. The Court granted the motion.
questions: Are the procedures for appealing impoundments outlined in §46.55 the exclusive remedy for unlawful impoundments?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court concluded that §46.55 does not abrogate common law claims of conversion and therefore does not bar Potter’s action insofar as §46.55 does not contain any explicit language declaring itself the exclusive remedy for unlawful impoundments and does not otherwise indicate that the legislature intended for it to be an exclusive remedy. Thus, the Court remanded the case to the trial court.

title: Wynn v. Earin
facts: Respondent Pardner Wynn filed suit against petitioner Jolene Earin, his former therapist and marriage counselor, after Earin testified on behalf of Wynn’s former wife and provided information obtained during joint marriage counseling sessions at a hearing to determine child placement. The trial court ruled that although the witness immunity rule precluded Earin from being held liable for her appearance and testimony at the hearing to determine child placement, Earin had violated the Healthcare Information Act (Washington Revised Code §70.02) by disclosing information obtained during the joint marriage counseling sessions to the guardian ad litem that had been appointed for the children without being provided a formal release and by handling Wynn’s records in a negligent manner that resulted in their being stolen and the jury awarded Wynn damages accordingly. Wynn subsequently appealed the trial court’s ruling that the witness immunity rule precluded Earin from being held liable for her appearance and testimony at the hearing to determine child placement. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court, holding that Wynn’s claims relating to Earin’s appearance and testimony at the hearing to determine child placement are not barred insofar as the Healthcare Information Act abrogates Earin’s immunity under the witness immunity rule. Earin appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the witness immunity rule bar Wynn’s claim against Earin arising from her appearance and testimony at the hearing to determine child placement?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although the Healthcare Information Act abrogates the witness immunity rule, it does not do so in all cases involving information acquired in a pre-litigation professional relationship formed for non-litigation purposes. Thus, the Court held that Wynn’s claim against Earin arising from Earin’s appearance and testimony at the hearing to determine child placement is nonetheless barred insofar as the claim is not related to Earin’s individual treatment of Wynn and insofar as Wynn failed to object to Earin’s presence or testimony at the hearing to determine child placement on any ground implicating the rights conferred by the Healthcare Information Act.

title: Olver v. Fowler
facts: Petitioner Julie Fowler and Respondent Michael Olver were appointed special administrators of the estates of a couple involved in a committed intimate relationship after both partners died in a traffic accident. Since the couple was not legally married, there was contention on how the shared assets would be divided. After a court order for binding mediation, the mediator concluded that even though majority of the assets were in the male partner’s name, the female partner was entitled to 50 percent of his assets and ordered the transfer. The day before presentation to the Superior Court for King County a father to one of the children who survived the accident was granted a motion to intervene, contesting the law does not allow application of meretricious relationship doctrine (law of committed intimate relationships) where both partners are deceased. Furthermore, he argued if the doctrine did apply, the surviving child would be unjustly shielded from gaining access to the male partner’s assets if she prevailed in her liability claim. The Superior Court ordered 50 percent of the male’s assets be disbursed to the female’s estate, and explained the legal effect of a committed intimate partner relationship upon a tort creditor’s claim should be determined in the context of the liability case. Petitioner Fowler, administrator of the male partner’s estate, joined with the father in the appeal of the trial court’s judgment. Respondent Olver, administrator of the female partner’s estate, cross-appealed arguing the trial court erred in granting the father’s motion to intervene. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s judgment, and the Supreme Court of Washington granted Fowler’s petition for review.
questions: Did the trial court abuse its discretion when it allowed a party asserting a tort claim against a couple’s property to intervene in an action between their estates? Can Washington’s law of meretricious or committed intimated relationships be applied where both partners are deceased? Can tort claims against one committed intimate partner be made against the other partner’s estate under a theory of joint tort liability?
conclusions: Justice Bobbe J. Bridge’s opinion for the Court affirmed the judgments and findings of both the trial court and the Court of Appeals. Specifically, that the trial court did not abuse its discretion when granting intervention to the father, and that Washington’s law of committed intimate relationships can be applied to divided assets between committed partners’ estates where both partners are deceased. Finally, since neither of the lower courts addressed the principles of joint tort liability being extended to committed intimate partners in this case, and instead concluded resolution of the issue is best for a separate suit filed against the female’s estate, the Court also declined to address the issue.

title: In re dependency of A.K.
facts: Petitioner A.K., a dependent child that had been placed in foster care, ran away from her foster home on several occasions. At the behest of the respondent Department of Social and Health Services, the Yakima County Juvenile Court exercised its inherent contempt power and sentenced A.K. to a period of detention in excess of that provided for by the juvenile contempt statute. A.K. appealed the juvenile court’s sanction to the Superior Court for Yakima County and the Washington Court of Appeals, both of which upheld the sanction. A.K. appealed the Washington Court of Appeals’ decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the juvenile court err in failing to consider the adequacy of statutory criminal contempt sanctions prior to exercising its inherent contempt power?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and vacated the sanction imposed by the juvenile court, concluding that the statutory criminal contempt sanctions provided for by Washington Revised Code §7.21.040 may be imposed to sanction violations of a dependency order and that the juvenile court erred in failing to consider the adequacy of these sanctions prior to exercising its inherent contempt power.

title: Washington v. Daniels
facts: Respondent Carissa Daniels was charged with homicide by abuse and second degree murder after her son died in her care. The jury subsequently found Daniels guilty of second degree murder but left the verdict form pertaining to the homicide by abuse charge blank. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed Daniels’ conviction on grounds that assault cannot be a predicate offense for second degree murder. The Washington Court of Appeals also held that the state of Washington may not retry Daniels for homicide by abuse insofar as the jury’s silence on that charge acted as an implied acquittal. The state of Washington appealed this part of the Washington Court of Appeals’ decision to the Supreme Court of Washington. Daniels cross-petitioned, asserting that retrying her for second degree murder would subject her to double jeopardy.
questions: Was the jury’s silence on the charge of homicide by abuse an implied acquittal? Would retrying Daniels for second degree murder subject her to double jeopardy?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the jury’s silence on the charge of homicide by abuse was not an implied acquittal insofar as the jury was instructed to leave the verdict form pertaining to homicide by abuse blank only if it was unable to agree. The Court also held that retrying Daniels for second degree murder would not subject her to double jeopardy insofar as constitutional prohibitions against double jeopardy only bar the state from retrying defendants whose convictions have been reversed when the reason for reversal was insufficient evidence.

title: In re disability proceeding against Keefe
facts: The respondent Washington State Bar Association’s disciplinary board initiated a disciplinary proceeding against petitioner John Keefe after Keefe allegedly failed to comply with court rules and failed to avoid a conflict of interest. Keefe represented himself at the subsequent hearing and conducted his defense in a manner that suggested that a lack of mental capacity. In particular, Keefe made a number of statements that reflected delusional and paranoid thinking and a lack of grasp of reality. As a result, the disciplinary board initiated a supplemental disability proceeding and suspended the disciplinary proceeding. After hearing testimony from a psychiatric expert who concluded that Keefe likely suffers from paranoid schizophrenia, the disciplinary board recommended that Keefe be suspended and transferred to disability inactive status, finding that Keefe’s mental state renders him incapable of practicing law. Keefe appealed the disciplinary board’s finding and recommendation, asserting that they were supported by insufficient evidence.
questions: Does substantial evidence support the disciplinary board’s finding that Keefe’s mental state renders him incapable of practicing law?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the disciplinary board’s finding and recommendation, concluding that the psychiatric expert’s conclusion that Keefe likely suffers from paranoid schizophrenia had a reasonable basis despite the fact that the psychiatric expert was unable to personally examine Keefe. The Court also held that the disciplinary board could reasonably find this mental disability renders Keefe incapable of practicing law. Thus, the Court ordered Keefe suspended and transferred to disability inactive status.

title: Department of Corrections v. Fluor Daniel, Inc.
facts: After a dispute arose between petitioner Fluor Daniel, Inc. and the respondent Department of Corrections regarding the terms of a contract to construct a prison, both parties agreed to binding arbitration. The arbitrator subsequently found in favor of Fluor Daniel and awarded it $5,997,645. Fluor Daniel submitted the decision to the Superior Court for King County for the entry of a judgment and also requested an award of pre-judgment interest for the period that elapsed between the arbitration and the judgment. The superior court granted Fluor Daniel’s request and awarded it pre-judgment interest, ruling that because the arbitrator’s decision could not be appealed, the damages awarded were fixed and interest began to accrue. The Department of Corrections appealed the award of pre-judgment interest and the Washington Court of Appeals reversed. Fluor Daniel appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is the prevaling party in a binding arbitration entitled to pre-judgment interest for the period between the arbitration and the entry of a judgment?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that unless the parties’ arbitration agreement states otherwise, interest does not accrue in the period between the arbitration and the entry of a judgment regardless of the finality of the arbitration.

title: Washington v. Frost
facts: Petitioner Joshua Frost was found guilty in King County Superior Court of six counts of robbery, one count of burglary, one count of attempted robbery, and two counts of assault for acting as a driver in several robberies. Frost appealed his convictions claiming the State showed prosecutorial vindictiveness, erroneous admission of his statements, and erroneous limitation of defense counsel’s closing argument that the state failed to meet its burden of proof as to any of the robbery offenses, and instead limited to arguing defense of duress. The Division One Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s judgment and rejected all of Frost’s claims. The Supreme Court of Washington granted review only on the issue of the trial court’s limitation of defense counsel’s closing argument.
questions: Did the trial court abuse its discretion by limiting the defense counsel’s closing argument to defense of duress, thus infringing on Frost’s Sixth Amendment right to counsel and his Fourteenth Amendment right to due process of law?
conclusions: Justice James Johnson’s opinion for the Court held that Frost’s constitutional rights to counsel and due process of law were violated when the trial court prevented his defense counsel from arguing in closing both that the State failed to prove accomplice liability as to the robbery counts and that Frost participated in the robberies under duress. However, the trial court’s abuse of its discretion did not taint the evidence before the jury as counsel’s argument was not evidence, and the jury was properly instructed on the State’s burden of proof in establishing accomplice liability. Thus, the Court affirmed Frost’s conviction concluding beyond a reasonable doubt that any reasonable jury would have convicted Frost even absent the trial court’s limitation on defense counsel’s arguments.

title: Washington v. Posey
facts: Petitioner Daniel Posey was charged with first degree assault and second degree rape. Although Posey was a minor at the time, the juvenile court was required to decline jurisdiction because first degree assault is a “serious violent offense” under Washington Revised Code §13.04.030. Following a trial in adult criminal court, Posey was acquitted of first degree assault but convicted of second degree rape and sentenced. Posey appealed, asserting that the trial court lacked the authority to sentence him insofar as he had been acquitted of the charge upon which its jurisdiction was based. Posey also asserted that the trial court erred in excluding from evidence an email written by the alleged victim in which she indicated that she would enjoy being subjected to sexual violence. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Posey’s conviction and sentence. Posey appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court have the authority to sentence Posey for second degree rape after he was acquitted of the first degree assault charge that led the juvenile court to decline jurisdiction? Did the trial court err in excluding the alleged victim’s email from evidence under Washington’s “rape shield” law (Washington Revised Code §9A.44.020)?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the case should have been remanded to the juvenile court once Posey was acquitted of first degree assault. However, the Court also held that the trial court did not err in excluding the alleged victim’s email from evidence given that it was not addressed to Posey and merely discussed potential sexual behavior.

title: In re personal restraint of Bowman
facts: Petitioner Jacob Bowman was convicted of second degree felony murder with the predicate crime of drive-by shooting. Bowman subsequently filed a personal restraint petition in the Washington Court of Appeals. It asserted that just as assault cannot serve as a predicate crime to second degree felony murder insofar as the assault is not independent of the murder, drive-by shooting cannot serve as a predicate crime to second degree felony murder insofar as the drive-by shooting is inextricably intertwined with the murder. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Bowman’s conviction. Bowman appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May the crime of drive-by shooting serve as a predicate crime to second degree felony murder?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that as the crime of drive-by shooting is unlike the crime of assault in that it does not require a victim, only reckless conduct that creates a risk that a person may be injured, it is independent of the crime of murder and therefore may serve as a predicate crime to second degree felony murder.

title: State v. Chhom
facts: While depositions of the charges against petitioners Chhom and Steever were pending under separate prosecutions, they were transported to a jail in Yakima County to serve sentences for misdemeanor convictions in municipal courts located in King County where the charges were filed. The jail services were provided to the municipal courts by Yakima County pursuant to the terms of an interlocal agreement. In both cases, the King County District Courts entered a judgment dismissing the prosecutions for violation of the time for trial rule. The Superior Court for King County affirmed the judgment for dismissal in the Steever case, but reversed the judgment in the Chhom case and reinstated the prosecution. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the Superior Court’s judgment in the Chhom case and reversed and remanded the judgment in the Steever case, holding that the time for trial period was not tolled while Steever was incarcerated in Yakima county. The cases were consolidated and the Supreme Court of Washington granted Chhom and Steever’s petition for discretionary review.
questions: Is a defendant detained “outside the county” for purposes of former CrRLJ 3.3(g)(5)(1995)(tolling the time for trial) when serving a sentence imposed by a court of limited jurisdiction within the charging county in a detention facility located outside the county?
conclusions: Justice Barbara Madsen’s opinion for the Court reversed the judgments by the Court of Appeals, holding in agreement with the District Courts’ rulings that a defendant is not held “outside the county” within the meaning of former CrRLJ 3.3(g)(5) when the defendant is sent outside the county to serve a sentence imposed by a court of limited jurisdiction within the county. The Court of Appeals erred in its interpretation of the provision when it considered the words “detained…outside the county” in isolation and referring solely to the geographical location of the detention facility. If read as a whole, it is apparent that former CrRLJ 3.3(g)(5) applies to circumstances when the defendant is under “foreign” jurisdiction. Thus, the rule for tolling the time for trial does not apply because Chhom and Steever were not detained “outside the county” while their charges were pending because they were under the supervision of courts within King County.

title: Washington v. George
facts: Petitioner Keith George was convicted on two counts of violating a no-contact order from which the charges originated separately in Renton and Kent municipal courts, but were tried together in King County Superior Court. George argued that the Renton court erred in resetting the time for trial after he failed to appear to two pretrial hearings because he was detained by the city of Kent and King County Disctict Court on unrelated charges. He also argued that his conviction on the charge initially violated the prohibition against double jeopardy because the Kent municipal court had dismissed the charge with prejudice before it was tried in Superior Court. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s judgment, holding George’s right to a timely trial was not violated. The Supreme Court of Washington granted George’s petition for review.
questions: Must the State demonstrate it exercised good faith and due diligence in attempting to procure a defendant’s presence in court in order to avail itself of CrRLJ 3.3(c)(2)(ii), which requires a trial court to reset the time for trial when a defendant failed to appear at a proceeding?
conclusions: Justice Barbara Madsen’s opinion for a unanimous Court held that the application of CrRLJ 3.3(c)(2)(ii) does not require due diligence on the part of the State. However, the Renton municipal court improperly reset the time for trial clock because the period George was detained on unrelated charges is treated as an exclusion from the time for trial calculation and not a “failure to appear.” Affirming the judgment by the Court of Appeals, the Court also held that the trial was within the applicable time for trial period, and that George was not placed in double jeopardy when the second charge was dismissed with prejudice.

title: Washington v. Bennett
facts: Petitioner Bruce Bennett was convicted of first degree escape in the Superior Court for Clallam County. Bennett subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that the instruction given to the jury regarding the burden of proof, which was first used in the case of Washington v. Castle, denied him due process insofar as it undermined the presumption of innocence. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Bennett’s conviction. Bennett appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the Castle instruction satisfy the minimum constitutional requirements of due process?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although language in the Castle instruction instructing the jury that “the law does not require proof that overcomes every possible doubt” and that it should find the defendant not guilty if it believes that there is a “real possibility” of their innocence is problematic, the instruction does not impermissibly shift the burden of proof. However, although the Court held that the Castle instruction satisfies the minimum constitutional requirements of due process, it instructed trial courts to henceforth use the standard Washington Pattern Jury Instruction.

title: Arkison v. Ethan Allen, Inc.
facts: Petitioner Arkison was the court-appointed chapter 7 bankruptcy trustee for Michelle Carter, who was injured in 2002 from a piece of furniture during the moving process by employees of a furniture moving company hired by respondent Ethan Allen Home Interiors. When Carter filed for chapter 7 bankruptcy that same year, she did not list the potential legal claim against Ethan Allen as an asset, and Arkison’s file to discharge Carter’s debts was accepted by the bankruptcy court and the case was closed. Three years later Carter filed the suit against Ethan Allen in King County Superior Court for the 2002 injury. Ethan Allen subsequently filed a motion for summary judgment arguing that judicial estoppel barred Carter’s claim on the basis of her failure to disclose the potential claim as an asset during her file for bankruptcy. The case was reopened, and Arkison argued Ethan Allen’s summary judgment claim could not use the judicial estoppel defense against a bankruptcy trustee, and moved to substitute himself as the real party of interest. The Superior Court granted Arkison real party of interest, but also granted Ethan Allen’s summary judgment against Arkison based on the judicial estoppel defense, thus dismissing the legal claim. After being denied the motion for reconsideration, The Supreme Court of Washington granted Arkison’s petition for direct review.
questions: May a trial court apply the doctrine of judicial estoppel against a bankruptcy trustee standing as the real party of interest?
conclusions: Justice Susan Owens' opinion for the Court concluded that a trial court may not generally apply the doctrine of judicial estoppel to bar a bankruptcy trustee standing as a real party from pursuing a debtor’s legal claim not listed as an asset in bankruptcy proceedings. The court has previously established that a bankruptcy trustee has a separate identity from the bankruptcy debtor, and thus cannot be judicially estopped based on inconsistent positions. The trial court thus abused its discretion, and the Supreme Court of Washington reversed the judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: In re detention of Ambers
facts: Pursuant to Washington Revised Code §71.09, petitioner Kevin Ambers petitioned the Superior Court for King County for a trial to decide whether he should be unconditionally released from his civil commitment as a sexually violent predator. In support of the petition, Ambers submitted a report and declaration from an expert in the field of sex offender treatment that estimated that, if released, he has a 36% likelihood of reoffending over a fifteen year period. The superior court ruled that Ambers failed to present a prima facie case for release. In particular, the superior court found that although the expert’s report constituted evidence of a change in condition, the 2005 amendments to §71.09 require that a sexually violent predator seeking unconditional release present evidence indicating not only that their condition has changed but also that they are safe to be at large in the community. Ambers appealed this decision to the Washington Court of Appeals, which certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the 2005 amendments to §71.09 impose a higher threshold of proof for sexually violent predators seeking unconditional release?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the superior court, concluding that the 2005 amendments to §71.09 were not intended to impose a higher threshold of proof for sexually violent predators seeking unconditional release. Instead, the Court held that the amended version of §71.09 continues to require merely that sexually violent predators seeking unconditional release present evidence indicating that they no longer meet the definition of a sexually violent predator. Thus, as the report and declaration submitted by Ambers indicates that he no longer meets the definition of a sexually violent predator, the Court found that Ambers is entitled to a trial to decide whether he should be unconditionally released.

title: State v. Recuenco
questions: Is imposing a firearm sentence enhancement based on a deadly weapon finding subject to harmless error analysis under Washington law, and if so, was the error in this case harmless?

title: In re personal restraint of Hall
facts: Petitioner Ronald Hall was convicted of assault in the Superior Court for Pierce County and sentenced to an exceptional sentence on the basis of the trial court’s finding that the aggravating circumstances of deliberate cruelty and multiple injuries were present. Hall subsequently appealed his sentence, asserting that, consistent with the United States Supreme Court’s decision in Blakely v. Washington, the 6th Amendment to the United States Constitution requires that issues of fact regarding the presence or absence of aggravating circumstances be decided by the jury. The Supreme Court of Washington vacated Hall’s sentence and remanded the case for resentencing within the standard range, rejecting the respondent state of Washington’s argument that violations of the rule articulated in Blakely are subject to harmless error analysis. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the United States Supreme Court, which reversed the Supreme Court of Washington and remanded the case for determination of whether the erroneous imposition of an exception sentence upon Hall was harmless error.
questions: Was the erroneous imposition of an exceptional sentence upon Hall harmless error?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court vacated Hall’s sentence and remanded the case for resentencing within the standard range, concluding that the error committed by the trial court in sentencing Hall to an exceptional sentence on the basis of aggravating circumstances not submitted to the jury could not have been harmless error insofar as there was no possibility that a jury would have reached the same findings of fact regarding the presence of aggravating circumstances given that the exceptional sentencing provisions in effect at the time gave sole discretion to find aggravating circumstances and impose exceptional sentences to trial courts.

title: Washington v. Boyd
facts: Petitioner Michael Boyd was charged with possession of child pornography in the Superior Court for Pierce County. Boyd’s computer, which allegedly contains tens of thousands of images of child pornography, was seized as evidence. Prior to trial, Boyd moved to compel the state of Washington to provide him with a copy of the computer’s hard drive to enable independent testing. The trial court denied the motion, ruling that Boyd only has a right to reasonable access and entering an order that Boyd’s attorney be granted limited access to a copy of the hard drive in a state facility. Boyd appealed the trial court’s order directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does Washington Criminal Rule 4.7 require that Boyd be provided with a copy of the computer’s hard drive?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the trial court’s order, concluding that Washington Criminal Rule 4.7 obliges the state to provide Boyd with a copy of the computer’s hard drive as a necessary consequence of Boyd’s right to effective representation and a fair trial. In particular, the Court held that given the nature of the evidence, effective representation requires a full and independent analysis of the computer’s hard drive and the images contained therein, which would not be possible under the constraints imposed by the trial court.

title: Washington v. Armendariz
facts: Petitioner Ismael Armendariz was convicted of third degree assault and violating a no contact order in the Superior Court for King County and sentenced to five months in jail to be followed by one year of community custody. The trial court also ordered that Armendariz have no contact with the victim for five years, the statutory maximum term for third degree assault. Armendariz appealed the no contact order, asserting that the trial court lacked authority under Washington Revised Code §9.94A.505(8), which authorizes courts to impose crime-related prohibitions and affirmative conditions, to impose a no contact order effective for the statutory maximum term for his third degree assault conviction. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Armendariz’s sentence. Armendariz appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §9.94A.505(8) authorize a court to impose a no contact order as a crime-related prohibition effective for the statutory maximum term for the predicate crime?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although §9.94A.505(8), unlike the provision that it replaced (former Washington Revised Code §9.94A.120(20)), does not expressly provide that a court may impose crime-related prohibitions effective for the statutory maximum term for the predicate crime, the legislative history of §9.94A.505(8) indicates that the legislature did not intend to effect any substantive changes to §9.94A.120(20).

title: Washington v. Nichols
facts: Petitioner Caleb Nichols was convicted of possession of methamphetamine in the Superior Court for Spokane County after a search of his person following a traffic stop revealed methamphetamine. Nichols appealed his conviction, asserting that the traffic stop was pretextual and that he had received ineffective assistance of counsel when his attorney failed to challenge its legality. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Nichols’ conviction. Nichols appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Nichols’ attorney ineffective in failing to challenge the legality of the traffic stop that led to the discovery of the methamphetamine on Nichols’ person?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Nichols’ attorney was not ineffective in failing to challenge the legality of the traffic stop insofar as the stop was not pretextual. In particular, although the police officer that made the stop noted that the automobile was being driven in a suspicious manner, the immediate reason for the stop was the driver’s commission of several traffic violations.

title: In re personal restraint of Mulholland
facts: Respondent Daniel Mulholland was convicted of six counts of first degree assault while armed with a firearm and one count of drive-by shooting in the Superior Court for Pierce County. The trial court ordered that Mulholland’s first degree assault sentences be served consecutively, ruling that under Washington Revised Code §9.94A.589(1)(b) it had no discretion to order that these sentences be served concurrently. After exhausting his direct appeals, Mulholland filed a personal restraint petition in the Washington Court of Appeals. It asserted that the trial court erred in ruling that it lacked discretion to order that his first degree assault sentences be served concurrently. The Washington Court of Appeals vacated Mulholland’s sentence and remanded the case for resentencing, holding that the trial court misinterpreted the law and could have ordered that Mulholland serve his first degree assault sentences concurrently. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does a sentencing court have discretion to order that sentences for separate violent offenses be served concurrently as an exceptional sentence? If so, was the trial court’s misinterpretation of the law a fundamental defect that inherently results in a complete miscarriage of justice?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although §9.94A.589(1)(b) requires that sentences for serious violent offenses be served consecutively, a sentencing court may order that such sentences be served concurrently as an exceptional sentence imposed pursuant to Washington Revised Code §9.94A.535 if it finds that mitigating circumstances are present. The Court also held that Mulholland demonstrated, as a petitioner seeking to obtain relief on collateral review must, that the trial court’s misinterpretation of the law was a fundamental defect that inherently results in a complete miscarriage of justice.

title: Crafts v. Pitts
facts: Petitioner David Pitts entered into a contract with Glen Cloninger to convey his interest in a parcel of land that he was leasing to Cloninger if Pitts either defaulted on the lease or the lease expired before Pitts exercised his option to purchase. The lease subsequently expired without Pitts either renewing his lease or purchasing the property but Pitts refused to convey his interest in the property to Cloninger. After Cloninger assigned his interest in the property to respondent Gordon Crafts and his wife Jaymie, the Crafts filed suit against Pitts for specific performance. However, Pitts had in the interim declared bankruptcy and had his debts discharged by the bankruptcy court. The trial court ruled that the bankruptcy court had not discharged the Crafts’ action for specific performance and ordered Pitts to quitclaim the property. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s decision. Pitts appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the Crafts’ action for specific performance discharged in Pitts’ bankruptcy?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the Crafts’ action for specific performance was not discharged in Pitts’ bankruptcy insofar as an alternative right to monetary damages could not compensate them for the loss of a unique parcel of land.

title: Washington v. Everybodytalksabout
facts: Petitioner Darrell Everybodytalksabout was convicted of first and second degree felony murder in the Superior Court for King County. Prior to his sentencing, an employee of the Department of Corrections interviewed Everybodytalksabout as part of her preparation of the presentence investigation report. After Everybodytalksabout was sentenced to life in prison, he appealed his conviction, which was ultimately reversed on grounds that the trial court erred in admitting certain evidence. Upon retrial, the trial court admitted testimony by the Department of Corrections employee regarding incriminating statements Everybodytalksabout made during the interview. After he was once again found guilty, Everybodytalksabout appealed his conviction, asserting that as his attorney was not present during the interview and as he had not been informed of his Miranda rights, he had been denied his right to counsel and testimony regarding the incriminating statements that he made during the interview should therefore not have been admitted. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Everybodytalksabout’s conviction, holding that Everybodytalksabout had not been denied his right to counsel insofar as the Department of Corrections employee had not deliberately elicited the incriminating statements during the interview. Everybodytalksabout appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Everybodytalksabout denied his right to counsel when he was interviewed by the Department of Corrections employee without his attorney being present and without being informed of his Miranda rights?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Everybodytalksabout was denied his right to counsel when his attorney was not present during the interview and he was not informed of his Miranda rights insofar as the interview was conducted for the purpose of preparing the presentence investigation report and therefore represented a critical stage of the proceedings and insofar as the Department of Correction employee conducting the interview deliberately elicited Everybodytalksabout’s incriminating statements. Thus, the Court reversed Everybodytalksabout’s conviction and remanded the case.

title: Washington v. Burke
facts: Petitioner Justin Burke was charged with the third degree rape of a child. At trial, Burke argued that the 15 year old girl told him that she was of legal age to consent, and that he reasonably believed her. The State contends that Burke, when given the opportunity to tell his side of the story, terminated his interview with the police without ever mentioning that he believed she was of age. Burke was found guilty of statutory rape in Snohomish County Superior Court, and subsequently moved for a new trial, arguing that the prosecutor violated his constitutional right to silence by commenting on his father’s advice to end the police interview and wait to speak to counsel, and his failure to report to the police the female’s declaration of age. The trial court denied Burke’s motion, Burke was unsuccessful in his appeal to the Washington Court of Appeals, and the Supreme Court of Washington Granted his petition for review.
questions: Did Burke clearly and unequivocally exercise his right to remain silent, or did he maintain only partial silence during the police interview? Did the prosecutor improperly invite the jury to infer guilt from Burke’s exercise of the constitutional right to remain silent?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court held that because Burke’s interview with the police was pre-Miranda warnings and because he testified at trial, his Fifth Amendment right to silence was not violated when the State used his silence to impeach him. However, the State did improperly invite the jury to consider Burke’s invocation of the right to counsel at the interview to be evidence of guilt, especially where the interviewing officer accepted Burke’s question if it was possible to speak with an attorney as an assertion of his right to silence, not just right to counsel. Since the comments made by the State prosecutor were not harmless beyond a reasonable doubt, and because Burke’s pre-arrest silence was improperly used as substantial evidence of his guilt, the Court reversed the lower courts’ judgments and vacated Burke’s conviction without prejudice to the State.

title: In re personal restraint of McCarthy
facts: Respondent Donald McCarthy was convicted of third degree assault with sexual motivation and sentenced to a minimum term of twelve months imprisonment and a maximum term of sixty months imprisonment. Prior to the expiration of McCarthy’s minimum sentence, the Indeterminate Sentence Review Board conducted a hearing pursuant to Washington Revised Code §9.95.420(3) to decide if he is eligible for release. After denying McCarthy’s request to be represented by an attorney, the board found that McCarthy is more likely than not to commit another sex offense if released and added twenty-four months to McCarthy’s minimum term. McCarthy subsequently filed a personal restraint petition seeking review of the board’s decision in the Washington Court of Appeals. It asserted that offenders have a right to counsel during hearings conducted pursuant to §9.95.420(3). The Washington Court of Appeals held that due process requires that the board decide on a case by case basis whether offenders are entitled to counsel to ensure fundamental fairness. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Do offenders have a right to counsel during hearings conducted pursuant to §9.95.420(3)?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that while offenders have a liberty interest at stake during a hearing conducted pursuant to §9.95.420(3) and therefore are entitled to minimum due process, this does not include a right to counsel. In particular, the Court held that a hearing conducted pursuant to §9.95.420(3) is analogous to a parole hearing and has adequate safeguards against serious risk of error.

title: Spokane School District #81 v. Cowles Publishing Company
facts: Nathan Walters died as the result of an allergic reaction to a peanut butter cookie served to him as part of a school lunch on a field trip sponsored by the respondent Spokane School District #81. After Walters’ parents indicated their intent to file a wrongful death claim, they and the school district reached a settlement. In the interim, the Spokesman-Review, a newspaper owned by petitioner Cowles Publishing Company, submitted a request pursuant to the Public Records Act (Washington Revised Code §42.56) for all records related to the school district’s investigation and possible settlement of Nathan Walters’ death. The school district denied the request on grounds that the requested records are privileged communications and attorney work product and therefore exempt from disclosure under §42.56. The school district then requested a declaratory judgment that the records are exempt from disclosure while the Spokesman-Review moved for an order to
questions: Are the requested records privileged communications and attorney work product and therefore exempt from disclosure under §42.56? May a state agency seek a declaratory judgment as to whether a requested public record is subject to disclosure?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the requested records are exempt from disclosure under §42.56 insofar as they were relevant to a controversy to which the school district was a party and would not have been available under the rules of pretrial discovery because they were protected either by the work product doctrine or because they reflected privileged attorney-client communications. The Court also held that §42.56 allows a state agency to seek a declaratory judgment as to whether requested public record is subject to disclosure.

title: Washington v. Bergstrom
facts: Petitioner Gordon Bergstrom was convicted of first degree unlawful possession of a firearm in the Superior Court for King County. At a subsequent sentencing hearing to determine whether Bergstrom should be placed on electronic home monitoring, Bergstrom argued pro se that the state of Washington had miscalculated his offender score insofar as some of his prior convictions arose from the same criminal conduct. After Bergstrom’s motion for a continuance to present evidence that his convictions arose from the same criminal conduct was denied, the trial court proceeded to sentence Bergstrom. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Bergstrom’s conviction but remanded the case to the trial court for resentencing and ordered that each party be allowed to present additional evidence regarding whether Bergstrom’s prior convictions arose from the same criminal conduct. Bergstrom appealed the part of the Washington Court of Appeals’ decision that ordered that the state be allowed to present additional evidence at resentencing.
questions: Did Bergstrom’s pro se argument that some of his prior convictions arose from the same criminal conduct constitute a specific objection to the calculation of his offender score that placed the state on notice that it needed to present evidence?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Bergstrom’s pro se argument was not a specific objection insofar as Bergstrom’s attorney did not object the state’s calculation of his offender score either in their pre-sentence report or at the sentencing hearing. Thus, the Court held that the state was not on notice that it needed to present evidence and that the trial court erred in failing to order an evidentiary hearing at which both parties would be allowed to present additional evidence.

title: Ventenbergs v. Seattle
facts: After the respondent city of Seattle enacted Seattle Municipal Code §21.36.030, which prohibits solid waste collection companies other than those contracted by the city from performing construction, demolition, and land clearing waste collection services, petitioner Josef Ventenbergs filed suit against the city in the Superior Court for King County, asserting that the ordinance violates the privileges and immunities clause of Article I §12 of the Washington State Constitution and impaired a contract under which Ventenbergs performed solid waste collection services in violation of Article I §23 of the Washington State Constitution. The trial court granted summary judgment for the city of Seattle, ruling that performing solid waste collection services is not a fundamental right protected by Article I §12 and that regulating solid waste collection is among the city’s police powers insofar as it affects health and safety and that the city may contract with whomever it wishes in exercising this power. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s decision. Ventenbergs appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §21.36.030 violate the privileges and immunities clause of Article I §12 by granting special privileges to the companies with whom it contracts to provide solid waste collection services? Is §21.36.030 a reasonable exercise of the city of Seattle’s police powers? Did the city of Seattle fail to comply with the bidding procedures established by Washington Revised Code §35.21.156? Did the city of Seattle’s granting of a monopoly to perform solid waste collection services exceed the authority granted to municipalities?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that as performing solid waste collection services is a municipal police power, granting special privileges to the companies with whom the city of Seattle contracts to provide solid waste collection services does not violate Article I §12’s privileges and immunities clause insofar as there is no fundamental right to perform a government service. The Court also held that §21.36.030 is a reasonable exercise of the city’s police powers given that the city proffered reasonable grounds, including environmental concerns and the establishment of uniform delivery standards, for contracting exclusively with select companies and that the city had not failed to comply with §35.21.156’s bidding procedures insofar as §35.21.156 only applies to a subset of solid waste collection services. Finally, the Court found that the city had not exceeded the authority granted to municipalities given that Washington Revised Code §70.95.020 permits municipalities to grant exclusive collection and disposal privileges via contract.

title: Twin Bridge Marine Park, L.L.C. v. Department of Ecology
facts: After beginning construction of a dry storage marina facility on coastal property pursuant to building permits issued by Skagit County, respondent Twin Bridge Marine Park, L.L.C. was ordered by the petitioner Department of Ecology to stop work and obtain a substantial development shoreline permit. Twin Bridge Marine Park subsequently reached a settlement with the Department of Ecology to avoid fines, obtained additional permits from the county, and resumed work. However, the Department of Ecology refused to recognize the county permits, reinstated the fine that had previously been imposed upon Twin Bridge Marine Park, imposed an additional fine, and ordered Twin Bridge Marine Park to cease all operations until a new substantial development shoreline permit was obtained. Twin Bridge Marine Park appealed the penalties to the Shoreline Hearings Board, which ruled that the dry storage marina facility constituted a new substantial development for purposes of the Shoreline Management Act (Washington Revised Code §90.58) and required a new substantial development shoreline permit, that Twin Bridge Marine Park violated its settlement with the Department of Ecology by resuming work, and that Twin Bridge Marine Park’s reliance upon permits issued by the county did not preclude penalties. Upon appeal, the Superior Court for Skagit County reversed the Board’s decision, holding that Twin Bridge Marine Park was not required to obtain any additional permits from the Department of Ecology given that the county’s issuance of building permits was contingent upon a determination by the county that the proposed dry storage marina facility was in compliance with the Shoreline Management Act and that the Department of Ecology could not impose penalties upon projects with valid county building permits and could only collaterally attack the issuing of such permits by filing an appeal pursuant to the Land Use Petition Act (Washington Revised Code §36.70C). The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the superior court’s decision. The Department of Ecology appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May the Department of Ecology penalize a project constructed pursuant to valid building permits issued by a county under the procedures established by the Shoreline Management Act?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the Shoreline Management Act confers upon counties exclusive authority to issue building permits for projects consistent with their shoreline master plans, that exercises of this authority cannot be reversed by the Department of Ecology, and that the appropriate vehicle for the Department of Ecology to collaterally attack the building permits issued to Twin Bridge Marine Park is an appeal pursuant to the Land Use Petition Act. Thus, the Court dismissed the fines and orders levied against Twin Bridge Marine Park.

title: Bellevue John Does 1-11 v. Bellevue School District #405
facts: The Seattle Times Company submitted a public records request pursuant to the Public Records Act (Washington Revised Code §42.56) to the respondent Bellevue School District #405 seeking copies of all records relating to allegations of sexual misconduct by teachers made in the last ten years. After the school district notified all current and former teachers whose records were gathered in response to the request, a number of them filed suit in the Superior Court for King County, asserting that their records were exempt from release under §42.17.310(1)(b) insofar as their release would violate their right to privacy. The trial court ordered the school district to release the records of those teachers whose alleged sexual misconduct was substantiated, resulted in some form of discipline, or was the subject of an inadequate investigation. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed in part and reversed in part, holding that in addition to the records of those teachers whose alleged sexual misconduct was substantiated, resulted in some form of discipline, or was the subject of an inadequate investigation, the records of those teachers whose alleged sexual misconduct was unsubstantiated were also subject to release and that only the records of teachers whose alleged sexual misconduct was shown by an adequate investigation to be plainly false were not subject to release. The teachers whose records were thereby ordered released appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §42.56 require the disclosure of the identities of teachers who have been the subject of unsubstantiated allegations of sexual misconduct?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that §42.17.310(1)(b) exempts from disclosure the identities of teachers who have been the subject of unsubstantiated allegations of sexual misconduct as disclosing their identities would violate their right to privacy given that it would be highly offensive and given that the public does not have a legitimate concern in their identities due to the unsubstantiated nature of the allegations. Thus, the Court held that although letters of direction seeking to guide future conduct that are issued by school districts to teachers that have been the subject of unsubstantiated allegations of sexual misconduct are subject to release, the names of the teachers involved and any other identifying information must be redacted.

title: Sherry v. Financial Indemnity Company
facts: Respondent Kevin Sherry was injured by an uninsured motorist, and subsequently sought confirmation of an arbitor’s award determining his damages for the injury in Pierce County Superior Court. Sherry’s insurer, petitioner Financial Indemnity Company (FIC), objected to Sherry’s proposed judgment, claiming an entitlement to offset its under insured motorist coverage obligation by the amount of personal injury obligation it had already paid to Sherry. Both Sherry and FIC explicitly waived any objection to the trial court’s deciding the offset issue during the confirmation action. The trial court entered a judgment in favor of Sherry in which FIC was permitted to take the full personal injury protection offset, less a proportionate share of Sherry’s attorney fees. On Sherry’s appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court’s judgment and remanded for entry of a judgment in favor of Sherry for the full amount of the arbitration award, holding that because Sherry was not fully compensated for his damages, FIC could not take the offset. The Supreme Court of Washington granted FIC’s petition for review.
questions: Can the same trial judge who confirmed the arbitration award also resolve coverage disputes between the insured Sherry and the insurer, or should such disputes be resolved in a separate declaratory judgment action? When does an insured become “fully compensated,” allowing an insurance company to reduce judgment on an arbitration award to account for insurance benefits the insured has already received?
conclusions: Justice Tom Chambers’ opinion for the Court concluded that since both parties orally amended their pleading to include prayer for declaratory relief, the trial court did have the authority and jurisdiction to resolve the offset dispute during the confirmation action. Also, in terms of offsetting previously paid personal injury protection benefits from underinsured motorist insurance benefits, “full compensation” does not mean the amount recoverable under underinsured motorist insurance after the reduction for the comparative amount. Instead, the insured party is fully compensated when they have made complete recovery of the actual loses suffered as a result of an automobile accident as determined by a court or arbitrator. Thus, the Court affirmed the Court of Appeals judgment that FIC has no right to an offset since Sherry had not yet been fully compensated, and the case was remanded to the trial court for further proceedings.

title: State v. Dion
questions: Did the juvenile court properly extend its jurisdiction beyond the defendant's 18th birthday?

title: In re personal restraint of Borrero
facts: Petitioner Aaron Borrero was convicted of kidnapping and attempted murder in the Superior Court for King County after robbing and abducting Leslie Lemieux at gunpoint during a drug transaction and subequently attempting to drown him in the Yakima River. After exhausting his direct appeals, Borrero filed a personal restraint petition in the Supreme Court of Washington. It asserted that his convictions violated the 5th Amendment to the United States Constitution’s prohibition against double jeopardy insofar as the evidence necessary to prove the kidnapping also proved the “substantial step” element of the crime of attempted murder.
questions: Did convicting Borrero of both kidnapping and attempted murder subject him to double jeopardy?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed Borrero’s convictions, concluding that although the state of Washington did not identify in its charging instrument what facts constituted the “substantial step” element of the crime of attempted murder, it is not necessary to assume that these were the same as the facts required to prove kidnapping. In particular, the Court held that as the facts establishing kidnapping are by themselves insufficient to establish attempted murder and as the facts establishing attempted murder are by themselves insufficient to establish kidnapping, Borrero was not subjected to double jeopardy.

title: Washington Citizens Action Welfare Rights Organization Coalition v. Washington
facts: In the 2000 general election, Initiative 722, which reduced the amount that property taxes may be increased from six percent to two percent, was passed by the voters. Litigation was immediately initiated that challenged the constitutionality of Initiative 722. While this litigation was pending, the sponsors of Initiative 747, which reduced Initiative 722’s two percent limit on property tax increases to one percent, succeeded in placing it on the ballot for the 2001 general election. However, prior to the 2001 general election, Initiative 722 was declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court of Washington in the case of Burien v. Kiga.
