The trial court also reversed the ruling on whether the state could amend the assault charge. The Supreme Court of Washington granted Hall’s direct appeal.
questions: Can the State, pursuant to CrR 7.8(b), move to vacate a conviction against a defendant’s objections? If so, do double jeopardy principles preclude the State from retrial without a defendant’s consent, specifically where the defendant has fully served his sentence?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court held that there is no limitation in the language of CrR 7.8(b) that precludes the State from seeking relief on behalf of a convicted defendant. However this does not control the trial court’s grant of motion for relief in these circumstances. Since hall opposed the State’s motion to vacate his conviction, the constitutional protection against double jeopardy precludes the State from retrying Hall. Thus, the trial court erred in granting the State’s motion to vacate Hall’s conviction. The Court reversed the order granting the State’s motion to vacate the conviction and file the amended information.

title: Washington v. Ramos
facts: Petitioner Felipe Ramos was convicted of second degree murder in the Superior Court for King County after a trial in which the jury responded to a special interrogatory that it did not unanimously agree that intentional murder had been proven beyond a reasonable doubt but that it did unanimously agree that felony murder had been proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Following the Supreme Court of Washington’s subsequent decision in In re personal restraint of Andress that assault cannot serve as the predicate felony for second degree felony murder, Ramos’s conviction was vacated by the Washington Court of Appeals and the case remanded to the trial court. On remand, the state of Washington charged Ramos with first degree manslaughter. Ramos moved to have the charge dismissed on grounds that charging him with first degree manslaughter would subject him to double jeopardy in violation of the 5th amendment to the United States Constitution insofar as the jury had impliedly acquitted him of second degree intentional murder and therefore of the lesser included offense of first degree manslaughter. The trial court rejected the motion and certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the jury’s response to the special interrogatory impliedly acquit Ramos of second degree intentional murder?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court’s ruling, concluding that there had been no implied acquittal as intentional murder and felony murder are alternate means of committing the crime of second degree murder and therefore the fact that the jury could not unanimously agree that intentional murder had been proven beyond a reasonable doubt did not constitute an implied acquittal given that the jury did unanimously agree that felony murder had been proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Thus, the Court held that the state may charge Ramos with the lesser included offense of first degree manslaughter on retrial.

title: Washington v. Codiga
facts: Pursuant to the terms of a plea agreement, petitioner John Codiga pled guilty to three counts of child molestation in the Superior Court for Grant County. After an investigation revealed additional prior convictions that had not been considered in calculating Codiga’s offender score and which increased Codiga’s standard sentencing range, Codiga was sentenced. Codiga subsequently moved to withdraw his guilty plea on grounds that he had not been accurately informed of the consequences of his plea insofar as the sentence that was imposed was outside of the standard sentencing range that he had agreed to. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Codiga’s conviction and sentence, holding that Codiga’s guilty plea had been knowing, intelligent, and voluntary given that a clause in the plea agreement specifically stipulated that the discovery of additional criminal history could increase the standard sentencing range. Codiga appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the increase in Codiga’s offender score as a result of newly discovered prior convictions render his guilty plea involuntary?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that as the change to Codiga’s offender score was the result of newly discovered facts that Codiga had failed to disclose rather than the result of an error in calculation, Codiga was bound by the clause in the plea agreement in which he accepted the risk of newly discovered prior convictions increasing his standard sentencing range regardless of whether he orally confirmed the clause to the trial court.

title: In re detention of Martin
facts: Prior to petitioner Sheldon Martin’s scheduled release from prison after serving consecutive sentences for a burglary committed in Clark County, Washington and kidnapping and attempted sexual abuse committed in Oregon, the Thurston County prosecutor requested that the attorney general petition the Superior Court for Thurston County to have Martin committed as a sexually violent predator pursuant to Washington Revised Code §71.09. After the attorney general initiated a commitment proceeding, the superior court rejected Martin’s motion to have the proceeding dismissed on grounds that only a prosecutor in a county in which the accused was convicted of an offense may commence or request that the attorney general commence a commitment proceeding under §71.09. Martin appealed the superior court’s order, asserting that the Thurston County prosecutor lacked jurisdiction under §71.09 to request that the attorney general commence a commitment proceeding insofar as his Washington conviction had occurred in Clark County. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the superior court, holding that language in §71.09 referring to the county in which the accused was convicted relates to venue rather than jurisdiction. Martin appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §71.09 grant jurisdiction to commence or request that the attorney general commence a sexually violent predator commitment proceeding only to prosecutors in counties in which accused sexually violent predators have been convicted of an offense?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that language in §71.09 referring to the county in which the accused was convicted relates to jurisdiction and establishes mandatory and exclusive procedures for commencing a sexually violent predator commitment proceeding. Thus, as Martin had not been convicted of any offense in Thurston County, the Court ordered the proceeding against him dismissed.

title: In re detention of Kistenmacher
facts: Petitioner Alfred Kistenmacher was ordered committed as a sexually violent predator pursuant to Washington Revised Code §71.09 after a trial in which a forensic psychologist testified on the basis of his examination of Kistenmacher that Kistenmacher is a pedophile and an exhibitionist. Kistenmacher subsequently appealed his commitment, asserting that he had been denied the assistance of counsel at all stages of the proceedings guaranteed by §71.09 insofar as his attorney had not been present at the psychological examination. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Kistenmacher’s commitment, holding that §71.09 does guarantee assistance of counsel at pre-commitment psychological examinations. Kistenmacher appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §71.09 guarantee assistance of counsel at pre-commitment psychological examinations? If so, was denying Kistenmacher assistance of counsel at his pre-commitment psychological evaluation harmless error?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals on alternate grounds, concluding that although §71.09 guarantees assistance of counsel at all stages of commitment proceedings including pre-commitment psychological examinations, the error was harmless insofar as there was no indication that the forensic psychologist’s conclusions or testimony would have been different had Kistenmacher’s attorney been present at the examination and as much of the forensic psychologist’s testimony mirrored Kistenmacher’s own deposition.

title: Washington v. Lilyblad
facts: Respondent Stephanie Lilyblad was convicted of telephone harassment in the Superior Court for Cowlitz County after threatening her children’s paternal grandmother during a phone conversation. Lilyblad subsequently appealed her conviction on grounds that the trial court had improperly instructed the jury with regard to Washington Revised Code §9.61.230’s intent requirement insofar as it failed to instruct the jury that the intent to harass must exist at the time that the defendant initiates the phone call. The Washington Court of Appeals vacated Lilyblad’s conviction and remanded the case to the trial court for a new trial. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Must the intent to harass exist at the time that the defendant initiates the phone call in order for phone harassment to occur under §9.61.230?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the intent to harass must exist at the time that the defendant initiates the phone call in order for phone harassment to occur under §9.61.230 insofar as non-premeditated harassment that follows legitimate communication does not implicate the same privacy concerns and the language of §9.61.230 indicates that the legislature did not intend for it to proscribe such harassment.

title: Washington v. Neff
facts: After police discovered a marijuana growing operation and a methamphetamine manufacturing laboratory in a garage located on his property, petitioner Roy Neff entered into an agreement with the respondent state of Washington to submit to a stipulated facts trial in exchange for several of the charges against him being dropped and was subsequently convicted of unlawfully manufacturing a controlled substance while armed with a firearm in the Superior Court for Pierce County. Neff appealed his conviction and the firearm enhancement, asserting that he had not waived his right to appeal as part of the agreement, that the firearm enhancement was not supported by substantial evidence, and that his attorney had provided ineffective assistance of counsel by counseling him to accept the agreement. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Neff’s conviction. Neff appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Neff waive his right to appeal when he entered into an agreement with the state to submit to a stipulated facts trial in exchange for several of the charges against him being dropped? If not, does substantial evidence support the firearm enhancement? Did Neff receive ineffective assistance of counsel?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although the agreement between Neff and the state did not waive Neff’s right to appeal insofar as the agreement was confusing and contradictory and not fully understood by Neff, the firearm enhancement was supported by substantial evidence given that the evidence was sufficient for a fact finder to conclude that the firearms in Neff’s garage were used to defend Neff’s marijuana growing and methamphetamine manufacturing operations. The Court also held that the decision by Neff’s attorney to counsel Neff to accept the agreement in exchange for several of the charges against Neff being dropped did not constitute ineffective assistance of counsel and was a legitimate tactical decision.

title: Champagne v. Thurston County
facts: Petitioner Gene Champagne filed suit against his employer, respondent Thurston County, in the Superior Court for Thurston County, claiming that the county’s practice of paying its employees any additional pay earned at the end of the month subsequent to the month in which it is earned violates Washington Administrative Code §296-128-035 and that he is therefore entitled to double damages under Washington Revised Code §49.52.070. The trial court granted summary judgment for Thurston County. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s decision, ruling that Champagne’s claim is not actionable under §49.52.070 as no wages that were due had been withheld from Champagne. Champagne appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the revised version of §296-128-035 apply retroactively to bar Champagne’s claim? If not, does §49.52.070 provide a remedy for wages untimely paid in violation of §296-128-035? If not, does delayed payment of wages give rise to liability under Washington Revised Code §49.48.010?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although the revised version of §296-128-035, which permits delays of up to a month in disbursing additional pay, does not apply retroactively to bar Champagne’s claim, §49.52.070 only provides a remedy in cases in which wages have been willfully withheld. The Court also held that Thurston County was not liable under §49.48.010 insofar as its application is limited to cases in which employees have been terminated.

title: Washington v. Eggleston
facts: Following a first trial in which the jury was unable to reach a verdict and a conviction following a second trial that was reversed upon appeal, a third trial resulted in petitioner Brian Eggleston being convicted of second degree murder and assault in the Superior Court for Pierce County and sentenced to an exceptional sentence. Eggleston subsequently appealed his sentence, asserting that collateral estoppel barred the respondent state of Washington from seeking an exceptional sentence predicated upon his knowledge of the victim’s status as a police officer given that the jury in his second trial had found that he had not known or reasonably should have known that the victim was a police officer and that the trial court had in any event erred in finding that his knowledge of the victim’s status as a police officer constituted an aggravating factor when the question had not been submitted to the jury. The Washington Court of Appeals vacated Eggleston’s sentence and remanded the case for resentencing, holding that although the jury’s finding in Eggleston’s second trial did not preclude the state seeking an exceptional sentence on the basis of Eggleston’s knowledge of the victim’s status as a police officer, the trial court’s finding of an aggravating factor and imposition of an exceptional sentence was inconsistent with United States Supreme Court’s decision in Blakely v. Washington, which held that aggravating factors increasing the penalty for a crime beyond the prescribed maximum must be submitted to the jury and proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Eggleston appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did collateral estoppel bar the state from seeking an exceptional sentence predicated upon Eggleston’s knowledge of the victim’s status as a police officer? If not, was the trial court required to submit the question of Eggleston’s knowledge of the victim’s status as a police officer to the jury?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that collateral estoppel did not bar the state from seeking an exceptional sentence predicated upon Eggleston’s knowledge of the victim’s status as a police officer given that the jury’s finding in Eggleston’s second trial that Eggleston had not known or reasonably should have known that the victim was a police officer was unnecessary and irrelevant insofar as the jury was not required to answer this question once it had found Eggleston guilty of second degree rather than first degree murder. However, the Court also held that the trial court’s finding of an aggravating factor without submitting the question to the jury was inconsistent with Blakely. Thus, the Court remanded the case to the trial court for resentencing.

title: Washington v. Davis
facts: Petitioner Anthony Davis was convicted of harassment, malicious mischief, violation of a protection order, fourth degree assault, and unlawful imprisonment in the Superior Court for Spokane County. By special interrogatory, the jury also found that Davis should have known that the victim was particularly vulnerable and incapable of resistance due to youth. Consequently, the trial court imposed an exceptional sentence upon Davis. Davis subsequently appealed his sentence, asserting that the trial court lacked authorization to submit a special interrogatory to the jury insofar as this deviated from the procedures stipulated by Washington Revised Code §9.94A.535, which placed responsibility for finding aggravating factors solely in the hands of trial courts, that were in effect at the time. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Davis’s sentence, holding that the trial court did not err in submitting aggravating factors to the jury during the guilt phase of the trial. Davis appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Were trial courts authorized to deviate from the exceptional sentencing procedures stipulated by §9.94A.535 during the period between the United States Supreme Court’s decision in Blakely v. Washington, which held that aggravating factors increasing the penalty for a crime beyond the prescribed maximum must be submitted to the jury and proven beyond a reasonable doubt, and effective date of the 2005 amendments to §9.94A.535?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and vacated Davis’s sentence, concluding that although Blakely had declared §9.94A.535’s procedures for finding aggravating factors and imposing exceptional sentences unconstitutional and although the 2005 amendments to §9.94A.535 enacted in response to Blakely had yet to take effect at the time of Davis’s trial, this did not authorize the trial court to simply create a new procedure as to permit trial courts to do so would sanction judicial usurpation of powers reserved for the legislature.

title: American Safety Casualty Insurance Company v. Olympia
facts: Respondent American Safety Casualty Insurance Company, surety for Katspan, Inc., filed suit against the petitioner city of Olympia in the Superior Court for Thurston County in an attempt to recover additional compensation for construction work that Katspan had performed for the city. The superior court granted summary judgment for the city of Olympia, ruling that American Safety Casualty Insurance Company had failed to comply with a provision in the contract between Katspan and the city of Olympia that requires that any cause of action under the contract be filed within 180 days of the close of the project. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the city of Olympia had implicitly waived its right to demand compliance with the provisions of the contract when it agreed to negotiate a settlement with American Safety Casualty Insurance Company. American Safety Casualty Insurance Company appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the city of Olympia implicitly waive its right to demand compliance with the provisions of the contract when it agreed to negotiate a settlement with American Safety Casualty Insurance Company?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the city of Olympia had not waived its right to to demand compliance with the provisions of the contract insofar as any waiver of such rights must be unequivocal and the city’s actions, in light of the fact that the city stated on several occasions in correspondence with American Safety Casualty Insurance Company that it reserved its right to demand strict compliance with the contract, were at best equivocal.

title: Washington v. Minor
facts: Petitioner Jacob Minor was convicted of unlawful possession of a firearm in the Superior Court for Grays Harbor County after possessing a firearm in violation of Washington Revised Code §9.41.040(1)(a), which prohibits those that have been convicted of serious crimes from possessing firearms. Minor subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that he had been affirmatively misled by the state of Washington with regard to the effect of his earlier conviction for burglary upon his right to possess firearms insofar as the order of adjudication and disposition that was entered following the conviction erroneously failed to indicate that the conviction barred him from possessing firearms. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Minor’s conviction, holding that Minor had failed to demonstrate reliance upon the erroneous order of adjudication and disposition. Minor appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the erroneous order of adjudication and disposition that was entered followed Minor’s conviction for burglary affirmatively mislead him to believe that he was permitted to possess firearms?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although ignorance of the law is generally not a defense, in this case Minor was affirmatively misled to believe that he was permitted to possess firearms by the fact that the box adjacent to the paragraph entitled “felony firearm prohibition” on the order of adjudication and disposition form was erroneously left unchecked. Thus, as no other notice of the firearm prohibition had been provided to Minor, the Court vacated Minor’s conviction and dismissed the underlying charge.

title: Christensen v. Ellsworth
facts: Petitioner Ed Christensen filed a complaint for unlawful detainer against respondent Richard Ellsworth after Ellsworth failed to make a rental payment and failed to respond to a notice to vacate the premises. The court entered an order of default and a writ of restitution when Ellsworth failed to appear. Christensen subsequently sought a default judgment based upon the order of default. Ellsworth responded by moving to vacate the order of default, asserting that the unlawful detainer action was prematurely commenced insofar as it failed to comply with Washington Revised Code §59.12.030(3)’s requirement that three days notice be provided period prior to filing an unlawful detainer action. In particular, Ellsworth maintained that although the unlawful detainer action was filed five days after Christensen posted the notice to vacate the premises, it was premature insofar as Washington Court Rule 6(a) excludes weekends and holidays in calculating time periods of less than seven days. The trial court granted summary judgment for Ellsworth, ruling that Christensen failed to provide sufficient notice as required by §59.12.030(3). Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed.
questions: Does Washington Court Rule 6(a)’s time computation rule apply to §59.12.030(3)’s requirement that three days notice be provided period prior to filing an unlawful detainer action?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and remanded the case, concluding that Washington Court Rule 6(a)’s time computation rule does not apply to §59.12.030(3)’s requirement that three days notice be provided period prior to filing an unlawful detainer action as this requirement is not one that deals with the mechanics of the operation of the superior court and the plain meaning of §59.12.030(3) indicates that its drafters intended for three days to mean three calendar days.

title: Washington v. Hicks
facts: Petitioner Phillip Hicks was convicted of murder in the Superior Court for Pierce County. Hicks subsequently appealed his conviction on grounds that he had been provided ineffective assistance of counsel when his attorney failed to object to the trial court informing prospective jurors that the respondent state of Washington was not seeking the death penalty and on grounds that during jury selection the sole remaining African American in the jury pool had been unconstitutionally dismissed via a peremptory challenge on the basis of their race. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Hicks’ conviction, holding that although the performance of Hicks’ attorney was deficient insofar as he had not objected to the trial court’s error in informing prospective jurors that the death penalty was not being sought in the case, the deficient performance was harmless. The Washington Court of Appeals also held that a prima facie case of racial discrimination had not been made with regard to the dismissal of the sole remaining African American in the jury pool. Hicks appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Hicks denied effective assistance of counsel when his attorney failed to object to the trial court informing prospective jurors that the state was not seeking the death penalty? If so, was the deficient performance harmless? Was the sole remaining African American in the jury pool unconstitutionally dismissed on the basis of their race?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although the performance of Hicks’ attorney was deficient, the deficient performance was harmless insofar as there was no indication that it affected the jury’s verdict. The Court also held that the trial court did not err in permitting the state to use a peremptory challenge to dismiss the sole remaining African American in the jury pool as the state provided plausible race neutral grounds for their dismissal.

title: Young v. Young
facts: After petitioner Judith Young brought an action to quiet title to a piece of property in her name and eject from the property respondent James Young, who was residing on the property while performing remodeling and repair work, James Young filed a counterclaim seeking damages for unjust enrichment. The trial court quieted title in Judith Young’s name and awarded James Young the market value of the improvements he made to the property minus the overhead costs that would have been incurred by a professional contractor in making the improvements but that he had not incurred. James Young subsequently appealed the trial court’s award, asserting that he is entitled to either the full market value of the services he performed or the increase in the value of the property attributable to his work. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court and remanded the case for an award in the amount of the full market value of the services James Young performed. Judith Young appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is James Young entitled to the full market value of the services he performed or should his award be reduced to reflect his actual costs?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that in cases involving quasi-contracts for the improvement of real property where the defendant agreed to the improvements and the claimant has committed no fault, the proper measure of damages is either the the full market value of the improvements or the increase in the value of the property attributable to the improvements.

title: Washington v. Magers
facts: Respondent Kha Magers was convicted of the second degree assault and unlawful imprisonment of his girlfriend in the Superior Court for Pierce County. As Magers had previously been convicted of second degree assault and first degree burglary, he was sentenced to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole. Magers subsequently appealed his convictions on grounds that the trial court had erred in admitting testimony regarding his prior convictions and previous instances of domestic violence against his girlfriend, that the statement made by his girlfriend to a police officer following the alleged assault and unlawful imprisonment was inadmissible hearsay rather than an excited utterance, that the trial court had erred in precluding him from informing the jury that he faced life imprisonment without the possibility of parole if convicted, that the testimony of the police officer who responded to the scene was inadmissible opinion testimony, that the prosecutor committed misconduct during her opening and closing statements, and that sentencing him to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole constitutes cruel and unusual punishment. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed Magers’ conviction and remanded the case to the trial court for a new trial with instructions that testimony regarding Magers’ prior convictions not be admitted and that testimony regarding previous instances of domestic violence against the alleged victim be accompanied by a limiting instruction. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court err in admitting testimony regarding Magers’ prior convictions and previous instances of domestic violence against his girlfriend? Was the statement made by his girlfriend to a police officer following the alleged assault and unlawful imprisonment admissible as an excited utterance? Did the trial court err in precluding Magers from informing the jury that he faced life imprisonment without the possibility of parole if convicted? Was the testimony of the police officer that responded to the scene inadmissible opinion testimony? Did the prosecutor commit misconduct during her opening and closing statements? Does sentencing Magers to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole constitute cruel and unusual punishment?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and reinstated Magers’ convictions, concluding that testimony regarding Magers’ prior convictions and previous instances of domestic violence against his girlfriend was properly admitted insofar as it was relevant to whether, as required to establish an essential element of the crime of assault, she had a reasonable fear of bodily injury and to assessing the credibility of her conflicting statements regarding Magers’ conduct. The Court also held that the statement made by Magers’ girlfriend to a police officer following the alleged assault and unlawful imprisonment was admissible as an excited utterance despite the fact that the statement was preceded by a deliberate falsehood as this falsehood did not necessarily indicate that the statement was not spontaneous. The Court also rejected Magers’ argument that the trial court erred in precluding him from informing the jury that he faced life imprisonment without the possibility of parole if convicted, finding that such prohibitions serve to ensure impartial juries. Finally, the Court also ruled that the testimony of the police officer that responded to the scene was admissible insofar as it provided context and did not constitute opinion testimony, that the prosecutor’s opening and closing statements were neither improper nor prejudicial, and that sentencing Magers to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole is not grossly disproportionate given the offenses committed and Magers’ criminal history.

title: State v. Eaton
questions: Whether a defendant may be convicted of cocaine possession when the charging document mistakenly listed amphetamine possession.

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Burtch
facts: Petitioner Jack Burtch was disbarred following a hearing before the respondent Washington State Bar Association’s disciplinary board, which found that Burtch had violated several rules of professional conduct when he testified falsely and presented false evidence during disciplinary proceedings and refused to pay restitution and return unearned fees to former clients. Burtch subsequently appealed the disciplinary board’s decision to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that he had not received a fair hearing insofar as the disciplinary board had improperly considered previous professional misconduct not formally included in the complaint against him, improperly denied him the opportunity to call expert witnesses, and improperly considered evidence regarding his general character and reputation and that the disciplinary board’s findings were not supported by substantial evidence.
questions: Did Burtch receive a fair hearing before the disciplinary board? If so, were the disciplinary board’s findings of fact supported by substantial evidence?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the disciplinary board’s decision, concluding that Burtch’s pattern of professional misconduct did not need to be formally included in the complaint in order to be considered, that the disciplinary board had not erred in refusing to allow Burtch’s proposed expert witnesses to testify as Burtch failed to demonstrate that the proposed expert witnesses were particularly knowledgeable in the rules of professional conduct, and that the probative value of evidence relating to Burtch’s general character and reputation outweighed its prejudicial effect and had therefore been properly admitted. The Court also held that the disciplinary board’s findings of fact were supported by substantial evidence and that the disciplinary board had properly found and weighed mitigating and aggravating factors in disbarring Burtch.

title: Washington v. Schwab
facts: Petitioner Dale Schwab was convicted of first degree manslaughter and second degree felony murder in the Superior Court for Snohomish County after killing a man in an altercation. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals vacated Schwab’s conviction for first degree manslaughter, ruling that convictions for both first degree manslaughter and second degree murder for a single homicide violate the 5th Amendment to the United States Constitution’s prohibition against double jeopardy. After the Supreme Court of Washington subsequently decided in In re personal restraint of Andress that assault cannot serve as the predicate felony for second degree felony murder, Schwab filed a personal restraint petition in the Washington Court of Appeals appealing his remaining conviction for second degree felony murder. As Schwab’s conviction for second degree felony murder had been predicated upon assault, the Washington Court of Appeals vacated the conviction and remanded the case to the trial court. The trial court then reinstated Schwab’s previously vacated conviction for first degree manslaughter and sentenced Schwab, ruling that the conviction could be reinstated insofar as it no longer subjected Schwab to double jeopardy once Schwab’s second degree felony murder conviction was vacated. Schwab appealed the trial court’s reinstatement of his conviction for first degree manslaughter, asserting that the law of the case doctrine precluded the trial court from reinstating the conviction. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Schwab’s conviction. Schwab appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the law of the case doctrine bar the reinstatement of Schwab’s previously vacated conviction for first degree manslaughter?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Schwab’s previously vacated conviction for first degree manslaughter could be reinstated once it no longer subjected him to double jeopardy as Washington Rule of Appellate Procedure 2.5(c)(2) restricts the law of the case doctrine and allows an appellate court to revisit an earlier appellate decision in the same case and in the interest of justice decide the case on the basis of the law at the time of the later review. Thus, as justice would be served by reinstating the first degree manslaughter conviction insofar as Schwab would otherwise not be held accountable for the homicide, the Court held that the Court of Appeals did not abuse its discretion.

title: In re personal restraint of Dalluge
facts: While serving a term of community custody following his release from prison, petitioner Amel Dalluge was arrested and taken to the Grant County Jail, where he assaulted several of the officers on duty. As a consequence, Dalluge was charged with and subsequently convicted of violating the term of his community custody requiring that he obey all laws. After unsuccessfully appealing his conviction, Dalluge filed a personal restraint petition in the Washington Court of Appeals that asserted that committing assault while in jail did not violate the terms of his community custody insofar as he was confined and no longer in the community at the time and insofar as Washington Revised Code §9.94A.625(3) states that periods of community custody toll during any period of time an offender is in confinement. The Washington Court of Appeals dismissed Dalluge’s petition, ruling that Dalluge was still subject to the conditions of his community custody at the time of the assault. Dalluge appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Are the terms of community custody automatically suspended by §9.94A.625(3) while an offender is confined?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although Dalluge’s period of community confinement tolled during the time he was in jail, he was nonetheless still subject to its conditions during this time given that the legislature likely intended for the Department of Corrections to retain supervisory power over offenders on community custody who are confined.

title: Washington v. Chavez
facts: Following a bench trial, petitioner Azel Chavez was convicted in juvenile court of attempted murder, robbery, assault, unlawful possession of a firearm, and taking a motor vehicle without permission. Chavez subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that juvenile defendants charged with serious offenses have a right to a trial by jury under the 6th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §21 and §22 of the Washington State Constitution and that the legislature’s failure to define the elements of the crime of assault violates the separation of powers insofar as it delegates definition to the courts. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Chavez’s conviction. Chavez appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Do juveniles charged with serious offenses have a right to a trial by jury? Does the legislature’s delegation of the definition of the elements of the crime of assault to the courts violate the separation of powers?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the use of bench trials rather than jury trials in juvenile cases is consistent with the more rehabilitative mission of the juvenile justice system and that despite the fact that recent amendments have eroded some of the distinctions between the juvenile and adult systems, the juvenile justice system remains sufficiently distinct from the adult system so as to make its denial of jury trials constitutionally permissible. The Court also held that the delegation of the definition of the elements of the crime of assault to the courts does not violate the separation of powers given that the legislature has explicitly made the common law supplemental to the code and therefore implicitly acquiesced in the courts’ definition.

title: In re detention of Lewis
facts: While petitioner David Lewis was awaiting retrial on a charge of rape, the respondent state of Washington petitioned the Superior Court for Columbia County to commit Lewis as a sexually violent predator pursuant to Washington Revised Code §71.09, citing an earlier rape conviction and alleging that Lewis is a pedophile. After the rape charge against Lewis was dismissed, a trial to determine whether Lewis is a sexually violent predator under §71.09 was held and Lewis was ordered committed. Lewis subsequently appealed his commitment, asserting that the state had failed to plead and prove that he had committed a recent overt act of sexual violence and that at the time the state petitioned to have him committed he was not, as required by §71.09, about to be released from total confinement insofar as he was unaware that the outstanding rape charge against him was about to be dismissed at the discretion of the prosecutor. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Lewis’s commitment. Lewis appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Lewis about to be released from total confinement for purposes of §71.09 at the time the state filed its petition? Was the state required by §71.09 to plead and prove that Lewis had committed a recent overt act of sexual violence?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that §71.09’s requirement that an offender’s release from total confinement be imminent does not require that an offender be aware of their impending release and that the state is not required to plead and prove a recent overt act of sexual violence in cases in which an offender has been continually confined since the commission of their predicate offense.

title: Washington v. Riofta
facts: Petitioner Alexander Riofta was convicted of first degree assault with a firearm in the Superior Court for Pierce County after a trial in which the victim identified Riofta as the man who had fired shots at him with a handgun. Riofta subsequently filed a motion with the trial court pursuant to Washington Revised Code §10.73.170(2)(a)(iii) requesting D.N.A. testing of the hat worn by the perpetrator of the shooting. The trial court rejected Riofta's motion, ruling that §10.73.170(2)(a)(iii) requires that the requested tests yield significant new information and that any information derived from D.N.A. testing of the hat would not be new insofar as the hat had been available for testing prior to trial. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's ruling. Riofta appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May §10.73.170(2)(a)(iii) be invoked to obtain D.N.A. testing of evidence that could have been, but was not, tested prior to trial? If so, did Riofta demonstrate, as required by §10.73.170(2)(a)(iii), a sufficient likelihood that the D.N.A. evidence could demonstrate the probability of his innocence?
conclusions: Justice Madsen's opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals insofar as it held that §10.73.170(2)(a)(iii) allows D.N.A. testing of any evidence that may provide significant new information regardless of whether the evidence could have been, but was not, tested prior to trial. However, the Court also concluded that Riofta had not demonstrated a sufficient likelihood that the D.N.A. evidence could demonstrate the probability of his innocence as test results indicating that Riofta had not worn the hat and/or that someone other than Riofta had worn the hat would not necessarily demonstrate the probability of Riofta's innocence insofar as there was reason to believe that Riofta had only worn the hat for a short period of time and was unlikely to have left D.N.A. evidence linking him to the hat and insofar as the hat belonged to another person and the presence of D.N.A. other than Riofta's on the hat would therefore not necessarily exonerate Riofta. Thus, the Court affirmed the trial court's rejection of Riofta's motion.

title: In re personal restraint of Richey
facts: Petitioner Thomas Richey filed a motion in the Superior Court for Pierce County to vacate his conviction for the crime of attempted first degree murder and the subsequent exceptional sentences of 65 years imprisonment imposed concurrently with his guilty plea of first degree murder. Richey contends that the judgment and sentence for attempted first degree felony murder is facially invalid, and that his petition is not time-barred as the State alleged. Additionally, he contends that the trial court did not present valid reasons for imposing exceptional sentences for attempted first degree murder and first degree murder. The motion was transferred to the Supreme Court of Washington for review as a personal restraint petition.
questions: Does the crime of “attempted first degree felony murder” exist in the State of Washington? Did the trial court err in imposing exceptional sentences for both convictions? Is Richey’s petition time-barred according to Revised Code of Washington §10.73.090(l)?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for a unanimous Court held that since nearly every other jurisdiction has concluded the crime of attempted first degree felony murder does not exist, is it also a nonexisting crime in Washington. Nevertheless, Richey’s judgment and sentence remain facially valid because of his guilty plea in the alternative to first degree intentional murder and/or attempted first degree felony murder. Since the judgment and sentence are facially valid, Richey’s collateral attack petition is time-barred pursuant to the one-year time limit in Wash. Rev. Code §10.73.090(1). In light of the fact that the motion was time-barred, the Court declined to address the exceptional sentences issue and dismissed Richey’s personal restraint petition.

title: Washington v. Knight
facts: Respondent Alyssa Knight pled guilty to conspiracy to commit second degree robbery, conspiracy to commit first degree burglary, and second degree murder in the Superior Court for Spokane County. Knight subsequently appealed her convictions for conspiracy to commit second degree robbery and conspiracy to commit first degree burglary on grounds that they represented multiple convictions for a single unit of prosecution and therefore violated the 5th Amendment to the United States Constitution’s prohibition against double jeopardy. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed Knight’s conviction for conspiracy to commit first degree burglary and remanded the case to the trial court for resentencing. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did convicting Knight of both conspiracy to commit second degree robbery and conspiracy to commit first degree burglary subject her to double jeopardy? If so, does reversing Knight’s conviction for conspiracy to commit first degree burglary require voiding the entire plea agreement?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that convicting Knight of both conspiracy to commit second degree robbery and conspiracy to commit first degree burglary subjected her to double jeopardy insofar as both convictions arose from the same conspiracy. The Court also held that Knight’s conviction for conspiracy to commit first degree burglary could be reversed without voiding the entire plea agreement regardless of the fact that the language of the plea agreement stipulates that it is indivisible as the terms of plea agreements cannot limit the ability of the Court to reverse unconstitutional convictions.

title: Fisk v. Kirkland
facts: Petitioner Calvin Fisk filed suit against the respondent city of Kirkland in the Superior Court for King County after a city fire hydrant’s insufficient water pressure prevented the city from extinguishing a fire that ultimately destroyed his recreational vehicle. The trial court granted summary judgment for the city of Kirkland, ruling that the city owed Fisk no duty to provide water for fire suppression purposes. Fisk appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Under Washington Revised Code §80.28.010(2), which requires that all water companies furnish and supply service, instrumentalities, and facilities as shall be safe, adequate, and efficient, did the city of Kirkland owe Fisk a duty to provide sufficient water for fire suppression purposes?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court, concluding that although the water system operated by the city of Kirkland is a water company for purposes of §80.28.010(2), the city of Kirkland owed Fisk no duty under §80.28.010(2) as Fisk is not within the class of persons intended to be protected by the statute given that the duties it creates apply only to water companies providing services for hire and the legislature did not intend to impose liability for the failure to provide water for fire suppression.

title: Washington v. Warren
facts: Petitioner Richard Warren was convicted in separate trials of one count of first degree child molestation of his younger stepdaughter and three counts of second degree child rape of his older stepdaughter in the Superior Court for King County. Warren subsequently appealed his convictions, asserting that the prosecutor committed misconduct during closing arguments in both trials by mischaracterizing the state’s burden of proof, by referring to facts not in evidence, by disparaging defense counsel, and by improperly vouching for the testimony of one of the alleged victims. Warren also appealed the trial court’s issuing of a no contact order as a condition of his sentence prohibiting him for life from having contact with his wife, asserting that it infringed upon his constitutional right to marriage. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Warren’s convictions and the no contact order. Warren appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the prosecutor’s statements during closing arguments constitute misconduct? If so, was the error harmless? Does the no contact order infringe upon Warren’s constitutional right to marriage?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although the prosecutor’s mischaracterization of the state’s burden of proof was improper, the misconduct was harmless insofar as the trial court subsequently issued an appropriate and effective curative instruction to the jury. The Court also held that although the disparaging statements made by the prosecutor with regard to defense counsel were also improper, there was no indication that they were prejudicial. Finally, the Court found that the no contact order prohibiting Warren from having contact with his wife is a valid crime related prohibition given that Warren’s wife is the mother of the two victims and given Warren’s previous conviction for domestic violence against his wife.

title: Washington v. Abrams
facts: The petitioner state of Washington charged respondent Dustin Abrams with three counts of first degree perjury for knowingly making materially false statements during his criminal hearing for first degree murder. Abrams moved to dismiss the perjury charges, arguing that Washington’s perjury stature is unconstitutional because Wash. Rev. Code §9A.72.010(l), which defines “materially false statement," provides that materiality “shall be determined by the court as a matter of law.” The Grant County Superior Court entered a judgment dismissing the charges with prejudice, ruling that the perjury stature is unconstitutional because it directs the court, opposed to the jury, to determine materiality of the false statement underlying the charge. The Supreme Court of Washington granted the State’s petition for direct review.
questions: Is the State’s perjury statute, Wash. Rev. Code §9A.72.010(l), unconstitutional insofar as it requires a judge to determine the materiality of a false statement as a matter of law?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court, holding that the clause instructing a trial judge to determine the materiality of a false statement as a matter of law is unconstitutional. The United States Supreme Court has previously declared that the materiality of a false statement in a perjury prosecution must be submitted to a jury rather than decided by a trial judge. Seeing as the procedure violated Abram’s right to a jury trial on every element of the crime with which he was charged under Art I, Sect. 21 of the Washington State Constitution, the offending language was severed and stricken, but the remainder of the perjury statute was upheld. The Court remanded the case for trial with the issue of materiality to be submitted to the jury.

title: American Legion Post #149 v. Department of Health
facts: After receiving notice from the respondent Department of Health that it was violating Washington Revised Code §70.160’s prohibition of smoking in public places and places of employment by allowing members and guests to smoke in its facility, American Legion Post #149 petitioned the Superior Court for Thurston County for a declaratory judgment that §70.160 does not prohibit smoking in private facilities and that, if it does, it violates the right to privacy granted by Article I §7 of the Washington State Constitution, the privileges and immunities clause of Article I §12 of the Washington State Constitution, the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment to the United States Constitution, and is void for vagueness. The trial court granted summary judgment for the Department of Health. American Legion Post #149 appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §70.160 prohibit smoking in private facilities that are also places of employment? If so, does §70.160 violate the right to privacy granted by Article I §7, the privileges and immunities clause of Article I §12, or the equal protection clause? Is §70.160 void for vagueness?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court’s decision, holding that §70.160’s exemption for private facilities occasionally open to the public is solely an exemption from §70.160’s prohibition of smoking in public places that does not modify its blanket prohibition of smoking in places of employment. The Court also ruled that §70.160 does not violate Article I §7’s right to privacy insofar as it implicates no fundamental rights, does not violate Article I §12’s privileges and immunities clause given that it does not prevent any entity from engaging in business, has a rational basis and therefore does not violate the 14th Amendment’s equal protection, and is not void for vagueness as it clearly prohibits smoking in any place of employment. Finally, the Court also concluded that American Legion Post #149 lacks standing in any event to bring a claim on behalf of its members as smoking is not germane to its purpose.

title: In re personal restraint of Bush
facts: After petitioner Jayson Bush had served seven years of a lengthy sentence for assault, Governor Gary Locke granted Bush a commutation of his sentence that released him from prison on the condition that he serve a term of community confinement and commit no gross misdemeanors or felonies. When Bush was arrested for assault two years later, Governor Christine Gregoire revoked the commutation. Bush subsequently filed a personal restraint petition in the Supreme Court of Washington that asserted that revoking the commutation without granting him a hearing violated his right to due process of law under the 14th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §3 of the Washington State Constitution.
questions: Did Bush have a liberty interest in the commutation of his sentence that precluded it from being revoked without due process? If so, was the revocation of Bush’s commutation without due process prejudicial?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court dismissed Bush’s personal restraint petition, concluding that although the commutation of a sentence does give rise to a liberty interest and therefore cannot be revoked without due process, Bush had not demonstrated that he had been prejudiced by the lack of due process insofar as he had stipulated to the accuracy of the police reports detailing the assault that he had been charged with and had not asserted any affirmative defense to the charge. Thus, as there was no indication that a hearing would have produced a different result, the Court held that Bush’s rights had not been violated by the revocation of his commutation.

title: Oltman v. Holland America Line U.S.A., Inc.
facts: Petitioners Jack Oltman and other cruise-line passengers who allegedly contracted a gastrointestinal disease while on a cruise sought damages from respondent Holland America Line U.S.A. Inc. for negligence, breach of contract, and fraud. Jack Oltman’s spouse Susan, who was not a passenger, asserted a claim of damages for loss of consortium. The King County Superior Court granted a summary judgment in favor of Holland America, holding that the forum clause in the passenger cruise contracts required suit be brought in the United States District Court for the Western District of Washington. The Oltman’s filed a motion to strike Holland America’s affirmative defenses regarding contract limitations because it was asserted in an untimely manner. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s judgment, and the Supreme Court of Washington granted the Oltman’s petition for review.
questions: Is the forum selection clause of the passenger cruise line contract valid and enforceable? Did Holland America waive its affirmative defenses by answering to the complaint in an untimely manner? Did the trial court abuse its discretion when it denied the Oltman’s motion to strike the affirmative defenses, as well as a declaration submitted by one of Holland America’s attorneys that may have been prejudicial to the Oltmans?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court held that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in denying the motion to strike Holland America’s affirmative defenses because the Oltman’s failed to prove it was prejudicial to their filing the claim in federal court. Nor did the trial court abuse its discretion in declining to strike Holland America’s attorney’s declaration that cited unpublished trial court decisions. However, the trial court did err in dismissing Susan Oltman’s loss of consortium claim because the claim is not subject to the forum selection clause since she did not sign the passenger cruise-line contract. Since the Oltman’s further failed to establish that the forum selection clause deprived them of their day in court, the clause is valid and enforceable. Thus, the Oltman’s were not entitled to file the suit in State court under the savings to suitors clause as they claimed. The Court affirmed the Court of Appeals on all issues except Susan Oltman’s loss of consortium, which was remanded to the trial court for further proceedings.

title: In re personal restraint of Dyer
facts: Following a parole hearing, the Indeterminate Sentence Review Board found petitioner Richard Dyer unparolable and increased his minimum sentence, concluding that Dyer was at risk to repeat the behaviors that resulted in his conviction for rape given that he continued to maintain his innocence and was therefore unable to participate in a sex offender treatment program. Dyer subsequently filed a personal restraint petition in the Supreme Court of Washington that asserted that the Indeterminate Sentence Review Board abused its discretion and violated his constitutional rights in denying him parole.
questions: Did the Indeterminate Sentence Review Board act within its discretion in denying Dyer parole on grounds that he was unable to participate in a sex offender treatment program? Does Washington Revised Code §9.95.009(3), which increased the weight attached to public safety in making decisions regarding parole, violate Article I §9 of the United States Constitution’s prohibition against ex post facto laws? Did the Indeterminate Sentence Review Board violate Dyer’s right to equal protection by conditioning his parole upon his eligibility to participate in a sex offender treatment program insofar as this is a factor beyond his control? Is §9.95.009(3) void for vagueness? Does the Indeterminate Sentence Review Board’s effective conditioning of Dyer’s parole upon an admission of guilt shock the conscience and therefore violate Dyer’s right to substantive due process under the 14th Amendment to the United States Constitution? Does Dyer’s continued indefinite imprisonment constitute cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the 8th Amendment to the United States Constitution?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Indeterminate Sentence Review Board’s decision to deny Dyer parole, concluding that the Indeterminate Sentence Review Board acted within its discretion in conditioning Dyer’s parole upon Dyer admitting guilt and participating in a sex offender treatment program. The Court also ruled that §9.95.009(3) is not an ex post facto law insofar as public safety considerations have always been given considerable weight in making decisions regarding parole and Dyer was given fair notice of the increased weight assigned to public safety by §9.95.009(3). Finally, the Court also held that conditioning Dyer’s parole upon participation in a sex offender treatment program does not violate Dyer’s right to equal protection as his inability to participate is not due to mental illness or other factors beyond his control, that §9.95.009(3) is not void for vagueness as it directs the Indeterminate Sentence Review Board in sufficiently clear terms to deny parole to those insufficiently rehabilitated, that effectively conditioning Dyer’s parole upon an admission of guilt does not shock the conscience, and that continuing to deny Dyer parole does not constitute cruel and unusual punishment insofar as the Indeterminate Sentence Review Board has not indicated that it intends to hold Dyer indefinitely.

title: Washington v. Becklin
facts: Respondent Andre Becklin was convicted of stalking after directing friends to follow his former girlfriend on several occasions. Becklin subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that the trial court had, in response to a question posed by the jury during its deliberations, incorrectly and improperly instructed the jury that stalking may be committed via a third party under Washington Revised Code §9A.46.110. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed Becklin’s conviction, holding that the trial court’s response to the jury’s question was an incorrect statement of the law and had come too late in the process to be a proper instruction. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May stalking be committed via a third party under §9A.46.110? Did the trial court err in responding to the jury’s question during deliberations?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and reinstated Becklin’s conviction, concluding that the direction or manipulation of third parties may constitute stalking under §9A.46.110 and that the trial court did not err in instructing the jury accordingly during its deliberations insofar as both parties had presented arguments regarding the factual validity of the state’s theory that Becklin had directed friends to follow his former girlfriend during the trial.

title: Futurewise v. Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board
facts: Following a decision by the petitioner Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board that the Shoreline Management Act (Washington Revised Code §90.58) continues to govern shoreline master plans adopted prior to enaction of the Growth Management Act (Washington Revised Code §36.70A), respondent Futurewise sought superior court review of the board’s decision. The superior court reversed the board’s decision, ruling that the Growth Management Act retroactively governs shoreline master plans implemented pursuant to §90.58 until the adoption of amended plans. The Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §36.70A retroactively govern shoreline master plans implemented pursuant to §90.58 until the adoption of amended plans?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the superior court, concluding that §36.70A was not intended to apply to existing shoreline master plans given the legislature’s intent in amending §36.70A to reverse an earlier board decision to the contrary and the reliance of local governments and property owners on existing shoreline master plans. Thus, the Court reinstated the board’s decision.

title: Sales v. Weyerhaeuser Company
facts: Alleging that his exposure to asbestos carried home by his father while his father was employed by petitioner Weyerhaeuser Company caused him to develop mesothelioma, respondent Charles Sales filed suit against Weyerhaeuser Company in the Superior Court for Pierce County. Weyerhaeuser Company subsequently filed a motion to dismiss the case for forum non conveniens on grounds that Arkansas is a more convenient forum than Washington given that the exposure to asbestos occurred in Arkansas and that Sales also received his medical treatment there. The trial court granted the motion. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the trial court should have conditioned its dismissal upon a stipulation by Weyerhaeuser Company that it would proceed in the state courts of Arkansas rather than remove the case to federal court given that removal would likely result in the case being transferred to a federal district court in Pennsylvania pursuant to the federal multidistrict protocol for asbestos cases. Weyerhaeuser Company appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Should the trial court have considered the possibility of the case being removed to federal court and subsequently transferred in deciding whether to dismiss the case for forum non conveniens?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the trial court should have considered the effects of the potential removal and transfer of the case upon the convenience of litigating the case in Arkansas rather than in Washington and could have conditioned its dismissal of the case for forum non conveniens upon a stipulation by Weyerhaeuser Company that it would proceed in the state courts of Arkansas rather than remove the case to federal court. Thus, the Court remanded the case to the trial court with instructions to take into account the potential effect of the federal multidistrict protocol for asbestos upon the convenience of litigating the case in Arkansas.

title: Livingston v. Department of Corrections
facts: Petitioner Michael Livingston, an inmate at Cedar Creek Corrections Center, filed a request with the respondent Department of Corrections for the training records of a corrections officer employed at Cedar Creek Corrections Center pursuant to the Public Records Act (Washington Revised Code §42.56). Upon receipt at Cedar Creek Corrections Center, the records were withheld from Livingston on grounds that institutional policy prohibited the release of employee records to inmates. Livingston subsequently filed a motion in the Superior Court for Thurston County asking the Department of Corrections to
questions: Did Cedar Creek Corrections Center’s withholding of public records from Livingston violate Livingston’s rights under the Public Records Act?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although a public records request may not be denied solely on the basis of the requester’s status as an inmate, the Public Records Act does not override Cedar Creek Corrections Center’s authority under §72.09.530 to design policies relating to the receipt of mail by inmates that are intended to maintain security and order.
